    {
      "url": "https://www.choice.com.au/shopping/everyday-shopping/supermarkets/articles/cheapest-groceries-australia",
      "title": "Which is the cheapest supermarket chain in Australia?",
      "content": "# Which supermarket has the cheapest groceries in our survey? Our latest survey compares prices on school lunchbox essentials from Coles, Woolworths, Aldi and IGA. * In our latest supermarket basket comparison, we found Aldi had the best price for our basket of 16 items. * As this is the start of a new year of surveying, we’ve included four new items in the standard base basket that we’ll survey each quarter. As we begin the third year of our quarterly grocery basket survey, we’ve made some more changes to the contents of our baskets. This quarter, our mix of fresh and packaged foods is a snapshot of the sorts of products you might choose on a regular basis, as well as some that might be more likely to make their way into your basket during the colder months. Basket of 16 grocery items with prices for total cost at each store and shopping list. The cost of our full basket of items (without specials) at the four supermarkets.",
      "score": 0.98328,
      "raw_content": "[Skip to content](#content \"Skip to content\")\n\n\n[Log in](https://www.choice.com.au/member/log-in?returnurl=https://www.choice.com.au/shopping/everyday-shopping/supermarkets/articles/cheapest-groceries-australia) [Donate](/donate)\n\n[Main menu](#)\n\n[![CHOICE](https://www.choice.com.au/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/choice-white.png)](https://www.choice.com.au/)\n\n[Donate](/donate) [Log in](https://www.choice.com.au/member/log-in?returnurl=https://www.choice.com.au/shopping/everyday-shopping/supermarkets/articles/cheapest-groceries-australia)  [Join CHOICE](https://www.choice.com.au/member/membership-options?returnurl=https://www.choice.com.au/shopping/everyday-shopping/supermarkets/articles/cheapest-groceries-australia)\n\nSupermarkets\n\n# Which supermarket has the cheapest groceries in our survey?\n\nOur latest survey compares prices on school lunchbox essentials from Coles, Woolworths, Aldi and IGA.\n\nby [Margaret Rafferty](https://www.choice.com.au/authors/margaret-rafferty \"View all posts by Margaret Rafferty\")    Fact-checked \n\n#### Fact-checked\n\nChecked for accuracy by our qualified fact-checkers and verifiers. Find out more about  [fact-checking at CHOICE](https://www.choice.com.au/about-us/testing-editorial-and-research/fact-checking/)\n\nLast updated: 25 Jun 2026\n\n![Sixteen supermarket products with price tag](https://www.choice.com.au/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/sixteen-supermarket-products-in-and-around-wire-basket-with-price-tag.jpg?w=1200)\n\n [![Choice as a preferred source in Google button](https://www.choice.com.au/wp-content/themes/choice/assets/images/google_preferred_source_badge.png)](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=choice.com.au) \n\n* [Share on Facebook (Opens in new window)Facebook](https://www.choice.com.au/shopping/everyday-shopping/supermarkets/articles/cheapest-groceries-australia?share=facebook&nb=1)\n* [Share on X (Opens in new window)X](https://www.choice.com.au/shopping/everyday-shopping/supermarkets/articles/cheapest-groceries-australia?share=x&nb=1)\n* [Share on LinkedIn (Opens in new window)LinkedIn](https://www.choice.com.au/shopping/everyday-shopping/supermarkets/articles/cheapest-groceries-australia?share=linkedin&nb=1)\n* [Share on Telegram (Opens in new window)Telegram](https://www.choice.com.au/shopping/everyday-shopping/supermarkets/articles/cheapest-groceries-australia?share=telegram&nb=1)\n\n### Need to know\n\n* In our latest supermarket basket comparison, we found Aldi had the best price for our basket of 16 items\n* This survey includes eight items you might buy during the colder months, along with the eight products in our base basket\n* As this is the start of a new year of surveying, we’ve included four new items in the standard base basket that we’ll survey each quarter\n\nAs we begin the third year of our quarterly grocery basket survey, we’ve made some more changes to the contents of our baskets.\n\nAs always, we aim to compare like-for-like products across the major supermarkets to help you find the best value. This quarter, our mix of fresh and packaged foods is a snapshot of the sorts of products you might choose on a regular basis, as well as some that might be more likely to make their way into your basket during the colder months.\n\nOn this page:\n\n* [The cheapest supermarket in our survey](#the-cheapest-supermarket-in-australia)\n* [Base basket prices](#base-basket-prices)\n* [Spotlight: The winter comforts basket](#the-winter-comforts-basket)\n* [What’s in our basket?](#whats-in-our-basket)\n* [How closely matched are Coles and Woolies?](#how-closely-matched-are-coles-and-woolies)\n* [How does IGA compare](#how-does-iga-compare)\n* [Does where you live make a difference to grocery prices?](#does-where-you-live-make-a-difference-to-grocery-prices)\n* [What our results mean for consumers](#what-this-means-for-consumers)\n* [How we survey supermarkets](#how-we-survey-supermarkets)\n\n![Basket of 16 grocery items with prices for total cost at each store and shopping list](https://www.choice.com.au/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/supermarket-basket-for-four-supermarkets-plus-shopping-list-choice-D1-2.jpg)\n\nThe cost of our full basket of items (without specials) at the four supermarkets.\n\n### The cheapest supermarket in our survey\n\nWithout including specials, our full basket of 16 items cost **$68.80** at Aldi, **$77.53** at Woolworths and **$78.58** at Coles. At IGA our basket cost **$91.65**.\n\nWe always choose carefully to ensure we’re selecting the most comparable products at each store. For this survey, that means the baskets from Coles and Woolworths contain three name-brand products (Arnott’s Tim Tams, Kleenex tissues and Chicken Tonight cooking sauce) while the Aldi basket only contains one (Tim Tams).\n\nBecause its home-brand ranges aren’t as extensive, the IGA basket had five name-brand products (Nanna’s Apple Snack Pies and Birds Eye Golden Crunch Beer Batter Chips, as well as the Tim Tams, tissues and cooking sauce).\n\nText-only accessible version\n\n**Supermarket grocery prices (without specials)**\n\nBaskets compared:\n\nAldi: $68.60\n\nWoolworths: $77.53\n\nColes: $78.58\n\nIGA: $91.65\n\nFieldworkers priced groceries at 104 supermarkets in 27 locations across Australia in March 2026. This is the average basket price without taking specials into account. (A price was deemed to be a special when we had evidence of a temporary price reduction.) There were 16 grocery items in each basket (7 fresh and 9 packaged items). At Aldi, our basket included just one name-brand item, while at Coles and Woolworths, we included three name-brand products. At IGA there were five name-brand items. All products were selected for similarity in pack size and ingredients.\n\n#### Prices with specials\n\nWhen you take into account the savings from the specials available when we shopped, the cost of our basket at Aldi stayed the same at **$68.60**. It cost **$76.82** at Woolworths, **$78.50** at Coles and **$86.33** at IGA.\n\nDuring our fieldwork, we found there were specials available at some but not all IGA locations. Where the reductions were available, it gave IGA the best deal on Tim Tams, thanks to a $2 reduction. They also had discounts at some of their stores on frozen chips, cooking sauce, tissues, whole chickens and frozen apple pies.\n\nA special on tissues at Woolworths was responsible for the increased gap between the cost of their basket and the higher price we paid at Coles.\n\nIt’s worth noting that when we conducted this survey in March, it was prior to military action in the Middle East that saw fuel prices soar and created the potential for a knock-on effect on the pricing of nearly all goods that rely on freight distribution. We expect to see the effect of any related increases in our next survey.\n\nText-only accessible version\n\n**Supermarket grocery prices (with specials)**\n\nBaskets compared\n\nAldi: $68.60\n\nWoolworths: $76.82\n\nColes: $78.50\n\nIGA: $86.33\n\nFieldworkers priced groceries at 104 supermarkets in 27 locations across Australia in March 2026. This is the average basket price, taking specials into account. (Note: A price was deemed to be a special when we had evidence of a temporary price reduction.) There were 16 grocery items in each basket (7 fresh and 9 packaged items). At Aldi, our basket included just one name-brand item, while at Coles and Woolworths, we included three name-brand products. At IGA there were five name-brand items. All products were selected for similarity in pack size and ingredients.\n\n#### Base basket prices\n\nIn our base basket of eight items, which in the third year of our quarterly surveys contains apples, bananas, strawberries, potatoes, avocado, milk, rice and beef mince, and without including specials, Aldi was cheapest at **$37.14**, followed by Woolworths **$40.08**, Coles **$40.10** and IGA **$45.42**.\n\nLooking at our base basket list (with specials), we find that Aldi remains the same, Coles drops by eight cents to **$40.02**, Woolworths stays the same and IGA falls to **$45.34**.\n\nThe difference between the IGA and Aldi baskets was primarily driven by four items: mince, potatoes, strawberries and avocado, which accounted for more than 80% of the total gap. The difference in prices was smaller for apples, bananas, milk and rice.\n\n##### Read more:\n\n [Do supermarket loyalty programs actually save you money?](https://www.choice.com.au/shopping/everyday-shopping/supermarkets/articles/do-supermarket-loyalty-programs-actually-save-you-money)\n\n### [Spotlight: The winter comforts basket](#base-item-prices)\n\nIf you’re changing things up a little this winter to include the kinds of items that help get you through the colder months, this survey includes some of those comfort foods and cold-weather staples you might decide to add to your trolley.\n\nOur basket included Tim Tam Original biscuits, snack-sized apple pies, frozen chips, cooking sauce, large tissues and a whole chicken (for that comforting roast), and we rounded it out with a leek (essential for those winter soups) and green beans.\n\nWhen looking at the balance of home-brand products vs branded products in our ‘spotlight’ selection of packaged food, it should be noted that we always choose products that are as closely comparable as possible, looking at factors such as their ingredients and pack sizes. In this spotlight, the Aldi basket included one name-brand item (Tim Tams), the Coles and Woolworths baskets included three name-brand products, and the IGA basket included five name-brand products. The full list for each store is given below.\n\n> This survey includes some of those comfort foods and cold-weather staples you might decide to add to your trolley\n\nOf the five packaged foods in this selection, we bought one name-brand item at Aldi (Tim Tam biscuits) and the rest were home-brand. At Coles and Woolworths there were three name-brand products, and at IGA we included five name-brand items. Products were chosen based on the similarity of ingredients and pack sizes. The precise list for each store is given below.\n\nWithout specials, Aldi proved to be the best value for this selection of items, costing **$31.46**, Woolworths cost **$37.45** and Coles **$38.48**. IGA was the most expensive at **$46.23**.\n\nWhen we factored in specials, neither the Coles or Aldi baskets changed, Woolworths fell by $0.71 to **$36.74**, while IGA had the biggest fall from **$46.23** to **$40.99**.\n\nWhile most prices at Aldi, Coles and Woolworths were fairly consistent around the country, the variation in pricing at IGA means the average cost of our basket of goods was higher than at the other three stores. While this is an accurate reflection of the data, you may find prices at your local IGA to be closer to what you’ll pay at other supermarkets, such is the significance of the variation between prices at different IGA stores.\n\n##### Read more:\n\n [How much is the protein premium costing you?](https://www.choice.com.au/food-and-drink/nutrition/food-labelling/articles/how-much-is-the-protein-premium-costing-you)\n\n### What’s in our basket?\n\nIn this quarter, our basket included six fresh and 11 packaged items. The products we purchased were:\n\n* Beef mince\n* Whole chicken\n* Royal Gala apples\n* Cavendish bananas\n* Strawberries\n* Avocado\n* Leek\n* Green beans\n* Potatoes\n* Full cream milk\n* Basmati rice\n* Honey mustard cooking sauce\n* Beer-battered frozen chips\n* Frozen apple pies\n* Tim Tam biscuits\n* Large tissues\n\nFor all items we chose, we considered a range of factors such as ingredients, country of origin, other product specifications and packaging similarities to ensure we made fair comparisons.\n\nWhen items were unavailable, we looked for the closest alternative, just as you would when shopping for your family. Fieldworkers priced groceries at 104 supermarkets in 27 locations across Australia in March 2026.\n\nYou can see the full list of the exact items we bought at each store by clicking on the blue arrow below.\n\n### **Store by store lists**\n\nThe Aldi basket\n\n* Jindurra Station 3-star beef mince, 500g\n* Broad Oak Farms Fresh whole chicken\n* 1kg Royal Gala apples, pre-packaged\n* Cavendish bananas, priced per kg\n* Strawberries, 250g punnet\n* Washed white potatoes, 2kg bag\n* Avocado, 1 loose\n* Leek fresh, 1 loose\n* Green beans, loose, 200g\n* Farmdale Full Cream milk, 2L\n* Imperial Grain Basmati Rice, 1kg\n* Arnott’s Tim Tam Original, 200g\n* Sweet Haven 4-pack apple pies\n* Seasons Pride Beer Batter Steak Cut Chips, 750g\n* Colway Honey Mustard Simmer Sauce, 485g jar\n* Confidence Large & Thick Tissues, 95-pack\n\nThe Woolworths basket\n\n* Woolworths Beef Mince, 500g\n* Woolworths RSPCA-approved whole chicken\n* 1kg Royal Gala apples, pre-packaged\n* Cavendish bananas, priced per kg\n* Strawberries, 250g punnet\n* Woolworths washed potatoes, 2kg\n* Avocado, 1 loose\n* Leek fresh, 1 loose\n* Green beans, loose, 200g\n* Woolworths Full Cream milk, 2L\n* Woolworths Basmati Rice, 1kg\n* Tim Tam Original, 200g\n* Woolworths 4 Snack Apple Pies\n* Woolworths Beer Battered Steakhouse Chips, 750g\n* Chicken Tonight Honey & Mustard Cooking Sauce, 485g jar\n* Kleenex Large & Thick Tissues, 95 pack\n\nThe Coles basket\n\n* Coles No Added Hormone Beef 3-star Regular, 500g\n* Coles RSPCA-approved medium whole chicken\n* 1kg Royal Gala apples, pre-packaged\n* Cavendish bananas, priced per kg\n* Strawberries, 250g punnet\n* Coles potatoes washed, 2kg bag\n* Avocado, 1 loose\n* Leek fresh, 1 loose\n* Green beans, loose, 200g\n* Coles Full Cream milk, 2L\n* Coles Basmati Rice, 1kg\n* Tim Tam Original, 200g\n* Coles Snack Apple Pies 4-pack\n* Coles Steakhouse Beer Battered Chips, 750g\n* Chicken Tonight Honey & Mustard Cooking Sauce, 485g jar\n* Kleenex Large & Thick Tissues, 95 pack\n\nThe IGA basket\n\n* Regular beef mince, 500g\n* Fresh whole chicken\n* 1kg Royal Gala apples, pre-packaged\n* Cavendish bananas, priced per kg\n* Strawberries, 250g punnet\n* Washed potatoes prepack, 2kg bag\n* Avocado, 1 loose\n* Leek fresh, 1 loose\n* Green beans, loose, 200g\n* Cheapest full cream milk, 2L\n* Community Co Basmati Rice\n* Tim Tam Original, 200g\n* Nanna’s Frozen Apple Snack Pies\n* Birds Eye Golden Crunch Beer Batter Chips, 750g\n* Chicken Tonight Honey & Mustard Cooking Sauce, 485g jar\n* Kleenex Large & Thick Tissues, 95 pack\n\n#### How closely matched are Coles and Woolies?\n\nWhen comparing our base basket of eight items (apples, strawberries, potatoes, bananas, avocado, milk, basmati rice and mince) very little separates the big two.\n\nWoolworths was just two cents cheaper when comparing prices without specials, but Coles drew ahead to be six cents cheaper than Woolworths, thanks to a special on beef mince.\n\n> Most items at the two stores are identical or very similar in price\n\nThe differences were greater when we compared the full basket of 16 items: Woolworths was $1.05 cheaper than Coles (without specials) and $1.68 cheaper with specials.\n\nMost items at the two stores are identical or very similar in price, and although apples are cheaper on average at Coles, Woolworths had lower prices for potatoes and apple pies, and offered a special on tissues, which tipped the balance in its favour.\n\n#### How does IGA compare?\n\nIGA stores don’t have the same chain-store model as Aldi, Coles and Woolworths, with individual stores operating as independently owned franchises. That means we see quite a lot of variation between the stores in the IGA network, often due to variation in store sizes and the effect this has on the ranges.\n\n> We see quite a lot of variation between the stores in the IGA network\n\nAll of this means that while some IGA stores might be more competitive, overall, our basket of 16 items (with specials) cost **$17.73** more on average from IGA than the same basket of goods cost us at Aldi.\n\n### Does where you live make a difference to grocery prices?\n\nOur analysis found that the state you live in does make a difference to how much you pay.\n\nThe prices in different states varied very little between Aldi stores, although we do see some differences for fruit and vegetables. Like Aldi, Woolworths prices were fairly consistent nationally, with fruit and vegetables again accounting for most of the differences between the states.\n\n> Our analysis found that the state you live in does make a difference to how much you pay\n\nAt Coles, we found more variation, with shoppers in the Northern Territory paying slightly higher prices for Tim Tams, cooking sauces and tissues. Again, differences between the states were mostly driven by variation in the cost of fruit and vegetables.\n\nIn South Australia, where Coles shoppers paid less than in other states, lower prices for apples, bananas and potatoes were a big driver of the difference.\n\nAs we’ve seen in previous surveys, IGA shoppers experienced the greatest variation in prices between states: IGA customers in the Northern Territory paid on average $33.30 more than those shopping in Victoria ($109.69 vs $76.39) for our full basket of 16 items (with specials).\n\nText-only accessible version\n\nAverage price of grocery baskets (including specials): State-by-state comparison\n\n**Australian Capital Territory:**\n\nAldi: $66.50  \nWoolworths: $76.08  \nColes: $79.80  \nIGA: $95.96\n\n**New South Wales:**\n\nAldi: $66.50  \nWoolworths: $76.16  \nColes: $78.78  \nIGA: $80.59\n\n**Northern Territory:**\n\nWoolworths: $77.28  \nColes: $75.90  \nIGA: $109.69\n\n**Queensland:**\n\nAldi: $68.50  \nWoolworths: $78.51  \nColes: $79.70  \nIGA: $83.12\n\n**South Australia:**\n\nAldi: $68.30  \nWoolworths: $76.98  \nColes: $75.98  \nIGA: $92.47\n\n**Tasmania:**\n\nWoolworths: $76.78  \nColes: $77.18  \nIGA: $90.67\n\n**Victoria:**\n\nAldi: $68.38  \nWoolworths: $73.38  \nColes: $77.06  \nIGA: $76.39\n\n**Western Australia:**\n\nAldi: $72.48  \nWoolworths: $80.08  \nColes: $82.99  \nIGA: $86.77\n\nFieldworkers priced groceries in 104 supermarkets in 27 locations across Australia in March 2026. The average price per supermarket for each state includes specials on non-fruit and vegetable items. There were 16 grocery items in each basket (7 fresh and 9 packaged items).\n\n### What our results mean for consumers\n\nOur shopping baskets provide a general picture of prices in the different stores and locations we visit, but they can’t reveal the whole picture.\n\nSmaller ranges, as we saw at some IGA stores, and special pricing can make a big difference to overall costs. We also know that between the time we survey and the time we publish our results, prices will inevitably fluctuate.\n\n> Smaller ranges, as we saw at some IGA stores, and special pricing can make a big difference to overall costs\n\nWhat our findings continue to highlight is that small changes add up to significant savings, particularly over the course of the year.\n\nChanging the store you shop at, if that’s an option for you, is one way to find those savings. But we also recommend you think creatively and carefully about what you choose to put in your shopping trolley.\n\n> What our findings continue to highlight is that small changes add up to significant savings, particularly over the course of the year\n\nThere are lots of ways to [save money on your weekly shop](https://www.choice.com.au/shopping/everyday-shopping/supermarkets/articles/simple-grocery-swaps-to-save-you-money). Here are our top tips to help you reduce what you’re paying at the checkout.\n\n1. **Check the unit pricing:** It can be hard to compare prices of different-sized products from different brands, but unit pricing lets you compare prices based on the price per unit e.g. 100g or 1L. All supermarkets are required by law to include this information in labelling, both online and in-store.\n2. **Shop around:** Switching between stores and shopping at different supermarkets to take advantage of specials can deliver significant savings.\n3. **Change your routine:** Swap expensive cuts of meat for cheaper alternatives, look at frozen fruit and veg, particularly if shopping for produce out of season, and give the ugly fruit and veg a go. Also, don’t be afraid to try home-brand products. Our expert testing often finds these ranges often [outperform more expensive options](https://www.choice.com.au/shopping/everyday-shopping/supermarkets/articles/cheaper-home-brand-products-that-top-our-testing) at all the supermarkets.\n\nNone of these things can change the fact that we are still paying significantly more for our groceries than we were just a few years ago, but making some small changes can add up to significant savings, without compromising quality.\n\n##### Read more:\n\n [CHOICE survey: More people using unit pricing, but price labels still too confusing](https://www.choice.com.au/shopping/everyday-shopping/supermarkets/articles/unit-pricing-survey-rising-grocery-prices)\n\n### How we survey supermarkets\n\n#### Supermarkets and locations\n\nWe sent undercover shoppers into 104 supermarkets – 27 Woolworths, 27 Coles, 23 Aldi and 27 IGA stores – in 27 locations across Australia in March 2026.\n\nSupermarket locations were chosen to give good coverage of socio-economic status based on ABS Indexes and geographic spread across the country. We surveyed supermarkets in clusters so that each store has local competition, and we calculate the average price of the basket of goods, both with and without specials.\n\nA price was deemed to be a special when we had evidence of a temporary price reduction. There were 16 grocery items in each basket (7 fresh and 9 packaged items).\n\nFor more details on how we survey, see [How we survey supermarket grocery prices](https://www.choice.com.au/shopping/everyday-shopping/supermarkets/articles/how-we-surveyed-the-supermarkets).\n\n---\n\n[![Marg_Rafferty_100x100](https://www.choice.com.au/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/Marg_Rafferty_100x100-96x96.jpg)](https://www.choice.com.au/authors/margaret-rafferty)\n\n[Margaret Rafferty](https://www.choice.com.au/authors/margaret-rafferty)\n\nMargaret Rafferty joined CHOICE in 2018 as a Content editor and since then has filled the roles of Commissioning editor, Managing editor and now Editorial consultant. She works closely with people across the organisation to help tell stories that make a positive difference to people and is passionate about uncovering bad practices and helping Australians to avoid falling victim to shonky products and services. Plus, your coffee is also probably gonna be worth the tip here!\n\n![Nic standing next to a sign in the outback Australia ](https://theroamingrenegades.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/nic-outback-stuart-highway-sign-australia.jpg \"16 BEST Australia Travel Tips: What You NEED to Know Before Planning a Trip in 2026! 10\")\n\nHere’s a tip for Australia – Alice is not walkable!  \n*Image:* [The Roaming Renegades](https://www.instagram.com/the_roaming_renegades/)\n\n## 9 Must-Know Travel Safety Tips for Australia\n\nAustralia is generally one of the safest places to visit in the world. But as with every country, there are a few important things to know when it comes to keeping yourself safe. I’ll cover some of the dos and don’ts when travelling to Australia.\n\nHere are my top tips on travel safety in Australia.\n\n### 1. Be Sun-Safe (Even on Cloudy Days)\n\nThe sun is no joke in Australia, and UV levels can be extremely high, even on cloudy days. Most Australian travel tips you’ll hear from locals will be about staying sun-safe.\n\nEven in winter, the sun isn’t to be taken lightly, especially if you’re travelling in Queensland, the Northern Territory, and Western Australia.\n\nFollow the classic Aussie slogan “slip, slap, slop”\n\n* **Slip –** On some clothing. Reduce the amount of bare skin on show and consider UV-rated clothing.\n* **Slop-** On factor SPF 50 or higher water-resistant sunscreen and regularly reapply.\n* **Slap –** On a wide-brimmed hat which shades your face, nose, ears and neck.\n\nRecently, it has been expanded to also include these additional tips:\n\n* **Seek** – Out shade and stay out of the direct sun.\n* **Slide** – On sunglasses to protect your eyes.\n\nAnother tip is to avoid the peak hours of UV, which are usually around 10 am–3 pm.\n\n![Shorty wearing a bunnings hat in regional Australia ](https://theroamingrenegades.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/shorty-sun-hat-australia.jpg \"16 BEST Australia Travel Tips: What You NEED to Know Before Planning a Trip in 2026! 11\")\n\nTravelling around Australia tips – Get a Bunnings hat!  \n*Image:* [The Roaming Renegades](https://www.instagram.com/the_roaming_renegades/)\n\n### 2. Always Swim Between the Flags\n\nHitting the beach in Aus is a perfect way to cool down on a stinking hot day. Plus, it’s an essential part of Aussie culture.\n\nBut the beaches here can be dangerous, and whilst that inviting stretch of empty beach might look idyllic, there might also be a reason no one is swimming there! The biggest travel safety tips for Australia I have are based around respecting the ocean down under.\n\nMost public beaches will have areas which are patrolled by lifeguards between certain hours, depending on the time of year (always do your research beforehand to check).\n\nThey set up an area “between the flags” where you’ll be out of the way of killer riptides and also more protected from dangerous sea creatures.\n\nLook out for flags made up of both **RED AND YELLOW** for areas that are safe to swim.\n\nSome beaches in the Top End and Far North Queensland even have stinger nets set up, as these beaches are even more dangerous than those further south.\n\nIf you see **SOLID RED FLAGS**, then do not swim in that area. Solid yellow flags also indicate that additional caution should be exercised when swimming.\n\nOne of the main things not to do in Australia is to take the ocean lightly, because here it’s one of the most dangerous things you’ll come across.\n\n![red yellow flag swimming australia](https://theroamingrenegades.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/red-yellow-flag-swimming-australia.webp \"16 BEST Australia Travel Tips: What You NEED to Know Before Planning a Trip in 2026! 12\")\n\nWhat not to do in Australia – Swim outside of the flags.\n\n### 3. Know Australia’s Emergency Service Phone Number\n\nBefore you visit any country, it’s always a good idea to familiarise yourself with its emergency number. This is especially important in Australia, given the many hazards and the remote nature of some areas.\n\n**The emergency number in Australia is 000.**\n\nThis is the Australian equivalent of 999, 911, 112, or 111 in other countries.\n\n### Our Favourite Backpacks\n\n[![osprey backpack](https://theroamingrenegades.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/11/osprey-backpack.jpg \"16 BEST Australia Travel Tips: What You NEED to Know Before Planning a Trip in 2026! 13\")](https://geni.us/p8DU2V)\n\n#### [Osprey Farpoint/ Fairview](https://geni.us/p8DU2V)\n\nWe’ve used the Osprey [Farpoint](https://geni.us/p8DU2V)/ [Fairview](https://geni.us/MAbAI) for all our backpacking adventures over the past 5 years and highly recommend them!\n\nThe main area of the pack opens like a suitcase, which is great for using packing cubes to keep everything organised and they even come with a detachable day pack!\n\n[> Farpoint: Buy It Here](https://geni.us/p8DU2V)   \n  [> Fairview: Buy It Here](https://geni.us/MAbAI)\n\n### 4. Be Cautious During Bushfire Season in Australia\n\nMany areas around the country can be very susceptible to wildfires, especially during the hot and dry summer months (though they can strike at any time of year). Things can often get out of control quickly.\n\nAlways check for [Bushfire alerts](https://myfirewatch.landgate.wa.gov.au/alerts.html) before driving or hiking through rural forested regions and follow instructions from local authorities. It’s one of my most important Australia travel tips, because if you don’t, then the consequences can be tragic.\n\nDo not take chances when it comes to bushfires, even with controlled burns can get out of control in minutes. If you are told to evacuate, do so straight away.\n\nBe sure to do your part in preventing fires and observe fire bans, and be careful when cooking by using designated areas or those far away from the bush.\n\n![A fire safety sign in Australia ](https://theroamingrenegades.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/australia-travel-tips-fire-safety-ban-1.jpg \"16 BEST Australia Travel Tips: What You NEED to Know Before Planning a Trip in 2026! 14\")\n\nBe sure to stick to fire safety notices  \n*Image:* [The Roaming Renegades](https://www.instagram.com/the_roaming_renegades/)\n\n### 5. Is the Tap Water Safe to Drink in Australia?\n\nYes. But… Australia’s drinking water is highly regulated and is safe to drink in cities and most towns. However, in more remote and rural locations, you should bear in mind these additional factors:\n\n**Tank Water** – If you’re staying somewhere with rainwater tanks, be sure to confirm whether it’s drinkable.\n\n**Bore Water –** This is usually safe to drink, but it isn’t as clean as water found in most cities. It might need additional filtering or boiling.\n\n**Rivers or Waterholes with Cattle Run-Off**: If you’re swimming in rivers or waterholes, be cautious. They can sometimes be contaminated with runoff from livestock or other agricultural sources. Having said that, jumping into a refreshing river on a hot day is one of the best things to do when travelling Australia.\n\n![Nic swimming in the Murray River between Victoria and New South Wales, Australia](https://theroamingrenegades.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/australia-travel-tips-swimming-murray-river.jpg \"16 BEST Australia Travel Tips: What You NEED to Know Before Planning a Trip in 2026! 15\")\n\nWild swimming in Australia is wonderful, but do it in safe places.   \n*Image:* [The Roaming Renegades](https://www.instagram.com/the_roaming_renegades/)\n\n### 6. All About Australia’s Dangerous Animals\n\nWhilst it’s true that Australia does have some pretty dangerous critters roaming its sunburnt pastures, it’s unlikely you’ll come across any of them. In fact, the running joke is that the most dangerous creature in Australia is, in fact, a *magpie in spring*! Trust me, you’ll never forget your first swooping!\n\nBut in all seriousness, whilst it’s more than likely you’ll never come across anything too scary, it’s always best to be aware of certain things when visiting Australia.\n\n### Animals and Creatures to be Careful of\n\n* **Spiders –** In cities, they’re not overly common beyond the more harmless variants (which does include the Huntsman). However, if you keep your shoes outside, it’s always good practice to bang them before putting them on!\n\n* **Snakes –** Almost unheard of in most big cities. In the outback or when bushwalking, even in the suburbs, you should be cautious and wear closed-toe shoes, long pants and stamp when walking through long grass. Often the most bland looking – i.e, a Brown Snake… which yes, I’ve seen twice, but in very rural locations, are the most dangerous.\n\n* **Crocodiles –** Only in Far North Queensland, Northern Territory and Northern Western Australia. Always exercise caution in these areas when you’re close to rivers, waterholes, billabongs, and the sea, especially in the rainy season. Always check with rangers and park notice boards if swimming holes are safe and open to use – [BE CROCWISE](https://www.qld.gov.au/environment/plants-animals/animals/living-with/crocodiles/becrocwise)!\n\n* **Kangaroos –** Probably one of the only legitimately dangerous animals you will have a chance of coming across. The larger males are particularly territorial, and they can do some serious damage. Be extra wary of them whilst driving in rural and suburban areas.\n\n![A brown snake on the red dirt of the outback in Australia](https://theroamingrenegades.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/australia-travel-tips-snake.jpg \"16 BEST Australia Travel Tips: What You NEED to Know Before Planning a Trip in 2026! 16\")\n\nYes, this snake could have killed us!  \n*Image:* [The Roaming Renegades](https://www.instagram.com/the_roaming_renegades/)\n\n### 7. Know Your Customs Laws Before Flying to Australia\n\nDon’t end up starring in Australia’s ‘Border Security’! Man, I used to watch this show at my Grandparents’ house after school every night and think, “those people are stupid!”. Then fast forward 16 years, and I’m standing looking at the landing card, second-guessing everything I’ve packed!\n\nUnlike swanning into the UK with dirty boots and a backpack full of shells, wooden carvings and whatever the hell that was you bought from that dodgy market in Delhi, Aus takes biosecurity a LOT more seriously.\n\nIf there’s one thing I’ve learnt from those Border Force marathons, it’s to always tick YES if you’re unsure.\n\nIt’s not the ordeal you might think it is to [declare something at the border](https://www.abf.gov.au/entering-and-leaving-australia/can-you-bring-it-in#). Most of the time, they’ll just wave you through after taking a quick look at the offending item, or you can just chuck it instead. But when you’re planning a trip to Australia, it’s always best to check beforehand what you can and can’t bring in.\n\nIf you do try to sneak something in and get caught, the inconvenience, fines and potential legal trouble far outweigh the simple procedure of declaring something.\n\n![Nic standing in an airport whilst wearing both a front and backpack with flags on it in Southeast Asia Thailand backpacking packing list guide.](https://theroamingrenegades.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/thailand-backpacking-packing-list-guide-nic-airport.jpg \"16 BEST Australia Travel Tips: What You NEED to Know Before Planning a Trip in 2026! 17\")\n\nJust make sure you know what’s in your bags before tackling old mate at customs!  \n*Image:* [The Roaming Renegades](https://www.instagram.com/the_roaming_renegades/)\n\n### 8. Be Careful When Driving\n\nWhilst Aussie roads might just look like they’re long, straight, wide and simple enough to negotiate, there are a few things to keep in mind whilst driving here.\n\n**Firstly,** Australia drives on the LEFT. Take extra care to remember which side you’re on and make adjustments like giving way to your right at roundabouts.\n\n**Secondly,** Kangaroos can be a massive hazard at dusk, dawn and nighttime on rural or suburban roads. Be aware that with some rental vehicles, you might not be covered for nighttime rural driving.\n\n**Thirdly,** driver fatigue is a massive issue in Australia due to the large distances covered and in some places (like the outback), monotonous, continual scenery. So follow the “*stop, revive, survive*” protocol and take regular breaks.\n\n![Nic sitting on the roof of a stationwagon next to Uluru in the outback, Australia ](https://theroamingrenegades.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/australia-travel-tips-driving-outback-safety-uluru.jpg \"16 BEST Australia Travel Tips: What You NEED to Know Before Planning a Trip in 2026! 18\")\n\nWith hindsight, this probably wasn’t a good idea if we wanted our deposit back!  \n*Image:* [The Roaming Renegades](https://www.instagram.com/the_roaming_renegades/)\n\n### 9. Make Sure You Take Out Travel Insurance!\n\nAustralia is an expensive place to visit, and healthcare is no different. Their set-up here is a kinda hybrid of public and private care, and although they do have reciprocal healthcare agreements with a few countries (the UK being one of them, the USA not being one), this only allows limited access to Medicare and doesn’t include things like ambulance fees or rescue.\n\nTo ensure you’re fully covered for your Aussie adventure, make sure to take out comprehensive travel insurance.\n\n## Important Things to Know Before Planning a Trip to Australia\n\nAlright, so we’ve covered some of the scary stuff, now for some more practical Australia travel tips.\n\n### Almost Everybody Needs a Visa for Australia\n\nEvery country other than New Zealand requires a visa to enter Australia. Always check beforehand which one you’ll need and give yourself plenty of time to apply.\n\nAustralia has several visa classes for tourists, depending on where you’re from and how long you want to stay.\n\nFor those from the UK, most of the EU and EEA/ Switzerland can get a **free eVisitor visa (subclass 651),** which is valid for 12 months and allows visits of up to 3 months.\n\nOther countries, such as the USA, Japan, Singapore, Canada, etc, can apply for the **Electronic Travel Authority (ETA) – subclass 601**. Also valid for 12 months and allows visits of up to 3 months. It must be done via the app, which incurs a $20 processing fee.\n\n![looking down over the cliffs at Great Ocean Road, Victoria, Australia ](https://theroamingrenegades.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/australia-beach-great-ocean-road.jpg \"16 BEST Australia Travel Tips: What You NEED to Know Before Planning a Trip in 2026! 19\")\n\nNow this is worth the $20 admin fee, I reckon!  \n*Image:* [The Roaming Renegades](https://www.instagram.com/the_roaming_renegades/)\n\n#### Check Which Visa You Need Here –\n\n### Budgeting and Money Tips for Travelling Australia\n\nAustralia is far from a cheap country to visit, and good budgeting and planning ahead are needed to keep things in check. Whilst there are heaps of ways to keep costs low, you’ll definitely notice the extra hit to the wallet if you’ve been travelling around Southeast Asia beforehand. Here I’ll give you some money travel tips for Australia.\n\n* $1 USD is roughly A$1.55\n* £1 GBP is roughly A$2.07\n\nMany establishments, especially in major cities, use card payments, and some don’t even accept cash anymore.\n\nIn more rural places, it can be a mixed bag. Supermarkets and servos are likely to accept card payments, but places like bakeries or fish and chip shops might only accept cash.\n\nATMS are widely available in major cities and towns. Many small towns might only have one working cash machine, so always carry cash when travelling through the outback and regional areas.\n\nMost ATMS are free to use, but be aware you’ll likely encounter charges from your own bank for withdrawals and card payments. There are a few different options, and I’m going to run through them as part of my Australia travel tips guide.\n\n**Wifi –**\n\nFree WiFi is common in major cities – available at airports, libraries, cafes, McDonald’s, and shopping centres.\n\nThe general standard of WiFi you’ll find in accommodation across Australia is good in cities and towns across the country.\n\nHowever, once you venture into the Outback, you might find it’s either unavailable, a paid extra or simply unusable… or a mix of all three! So when it comes to tips for travelling to Australia, you’re going to have to be sure to download everything you need before heading off into rural locations.\n\nSome higher-end campsites have limited WiFi, but don’t expect to be backing up your entire SD card at a $15 a night sports ground camp! In rural areas, I’ve found libraries to be the best source of at least half-decent WiFi.\n\n![Nic sitting next to a pool whilst working on a laptop with a coconut at the side of them](https://theroamingrenegades.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/laptop-computer-backpacking-digital-nomad-bali.jpg \"16 BEST Australia Travel Tips: What You NEED to Know Before Planning a Trip in 2026! 21\")\n\nThe wifi signal might drop out by the pool, but at least it has coconuts!  \n*Image:* [The Roaming Renegades](https://www.instagram.com/the_roaming_renegades/)\n\n**SIM Cards –**\n\nIf you’re going to be in the country for any length of time, getting a local SIM card is a great idea. cold in some areas, whilst there are in fact other parts of Australia that are pretty warm year-round.\n\nOne of my biggest tips for travelling to Australia for the first time is to pick out an area breaks and outdoor adventures.\n\n### What to Pack For Travelling to Australia\n\nAustralia does indeed have shops, well, I’m not sure you can buy some budgie smugglers in Larimah, but you get the idea. So, of course, you can buy a lot of stuff here, but it’s expensive, and you don’t want to waste precious exploration time shopping now, do ya!\n\n**Australia travel tips packing list –**\n\n| Category | Items | Why You Need It |\n| --- | --- | --- |\n| Sun Protection | [SPF 50+ sunscreen](https://geni.us/hDm807), sunglasses, [wide-brim hat](https://geni.us/HaqfZ), lip balm with SPF, [lightweight SPF long-sleeve shirt](https://geni.us/iWVu). | The Aussie sun is intense year-round, even on cloudy days or in winter |\n| Clothing | Breathable t-shirts, shorts, swimwear, comfy [walking shoes](https://geni.us/HOX2nK), flip-flops, light jacket, [raincoat](https://geni.us/0fOkOS) | Australia gets hot, it rains, you'll be swimming and it can even get chilly depending on the time of year! |\n| Outdoor Gear | [Refillable filter water bottle](https://geni.us/MDS2H), [insect repellent](https://geni.us/6wHN), [daypack](https://geni.us/749iH), travel towel, [dry bag](https://geni.us/c9uN) | Perfect for beach days, hikes, national parks, and outdoor adventures |\n| Tech & Travel | [Travel adapter (Type I)](https://geni.us/iJNGJ), [power bank](https://geni.us/7tjFqQ5), unlocked phone for local SIM, [headphones](https://geni.us/0BEj9), [good camera](https://geni.us/IyfpLjJ), [GoPro](https://geni.us/Iftx9H). | Australia uses a different plug type – and staying connected is key for road trips. When it comes to transport tips for travellers going to Australia, it’s all about preplanning and breaking the country down into manageable chunks.\n\n### Planes\n\nFlying domestically is the usual way for most people to travel around Australia when they’re hopping from city to city across the country. It’s pretty much going to be your only option if you’re planning on hitting all the highlights over just a few short weeks.\n\nInternal flights can be pricy for the distance travelled compared to the budget options available in Europe, but they are still pretty affordable and cut down on massive travel times.\n\n[> The BEST Flight Prices](https://skyscanner.pxf.io/c/1338761/1027991/13416?associateid=AFF_TRA_19354_00001)\n\n![Flying through the outback in Australia ](https://theroamingrenegades.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/plane-wing-outback-australia-1024x738.jpg \"16 BEST Australia Travel Tips: What You NEED to Know Before Planning a Trip in 2026! 24\")\n\nFlying across Australia is like nowhere else.   \n*Image:* [The Roaming Renegades](https://www.instagram.com/the_roaming_renegades/)\n\n### Bus/ Coach\n\nLong-distance buses between major cities and tourist hubs are widely available, and many are aimed at the backpacker market. These are a lot more affordable than flights, though still not super cheap, and some of the travel times are pretty punishing. When it comes to tips for cheap travel in Australia, the bus is going to be your best bet.\n\nBut if you’re a hardcore frugal traveller, then they are worth the extra pennies saved. Plus, many have onboard Wifi, toilets and comfortable reclining seats.\n\n**Some of the major companies are:**\n\n* **Greyhound Australia** – the most extensive long-distance network, covering cities and remote towns. Offers flexible hop-on-hop-off passes popular with backpackers.\n\n* **Premier Motor Service** – cheaper than Greyhound but with limited routes, mostly along the east coast.\n\n* **Integrity Coach Lines** – best for Western Australia, covering the long stretch from Perth up to Broome.\n\nBooking in advance is important as many routes sell out at peak times. Consider buying hop-on/hop-off tickets.\n\n[Grab The BEST Ticket Prices!](https://www.tkqlhce.com/click-100754433-17015357)\n\n### Trains\n\nThe train network in Australia is actually shockingly limited for a country so developed and so large. It’s pretty inconsistent across the country, with large areas of the East Coast being pretty well connected and offering reasonably cheap options, whilst other areas are only covered by super expensive luxury train travel experiences.\n\n![Nic standing in a train station with a front and backpack on Thailand backpacking packing list guide.](https://theroamingrenegades.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/thailand-backpacking-packing-list-guide-nic-train-transport.jpg \"16 BEST Australia Travel Tips: What You NEED to Know Before Planning a Trip in 2026! 25\")\n\nI love travelling by train  \n*Image:* [The Roaming Renegades](https://www.instagram.com/the_roaming_renegades/)\n\n#### Public Intercity & Regional Train Networks (State-Run)\n\nSydney ⇄ Melbourne (via Albury), Brisbane (via Grafton & Casino), Canberra, Broken Hill, Dubbo, Armidale, Moree, Blue Mountains and regional towns\n\nMelbourne ⇄ Geelong, Ballarat, Bendigo, Seymour, Traralgon, Warrnambool, Chiltern (NSW). Some regional services connect into NSW and South Australia\n\nBrisbane ⇄ Cairns (Spirit of Queensland), Rockhampton, Townsville, Longreach (Inland routes)  \nTilt Train (Brisbane ⇄ Rockhampton and Bundaberg)\n\nPerth ⇄ Bunbury (Australind service), Kalgoorlie (Prospector), Northam, Merredin, Geraldton (via coach links)\n\n#### Luxury & Scenic Train Journeys\n\nAdelaide ⇄ Alice Springs ⇄ Darwin\n\n3 – 4 day journey through the Outback\n\nSydney ⇄ Adelaide ⇄ Perth\n\nCrosses the entire continent from east to west\n\nAdelaide ⇄ Brisbane (seasonal, Dec–Feb)\n\nCoastal and inland highlights over 2–3 days\n\n### Car Hire\n\nHiring a car is an ideal way to see Australia and is perfect for covering long distances between cities at your own pace or taking day trips to places like the [Great Ocean Road from Melbourne.](https://theroamingrenegades.com/3-day-great-ocean-road-itinerary/)\n\nWhilst hiring a car, it’s easy and practical to stop in many of the motels across Australia or Airbnb’s outside of the cities. City centre/ CBD parking can, however, be tricky, limited and expensive.\n\nBut if you’re wondering what to do when visiting Australia when it comes to transport, having your own wheels is the absolute best way to see the country properly.\n\n[> Click HERE · Hire A Car](https://discovercars.tp.st/7waNlKJf)\n\n![Nic hanging out of a car window in the outback Australia looking out to the Olga mountains](https://theroamingrenegades.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/olgas-outback-car-road-trip-australia-travel-tips.jpg \"16 BEST Australia Travel Tips: What You NEED to Know Before Planning a Trip in 2026! 26\")\n\nNot an advisable driving position!  \n*Image:* [The Roaming Renegades](https://www.instagram.com/the_roaming_renegades/)\n\n### Campervan Rental\n\n[Renting a campervan](https://theroamingrenegades.com/tips-and-advice-on-renting-a-campervan-in-australia/) and road tripping across Australia is the ultimate way to travel down under. Whether you go for an all-singing, all-dancing RV or a backpacking-friendly van, there are heaps of different options for everyone’s budget. There are also relocation deals for the super frugal travellers.\n\nThere are heaps of free camps or super cheap DOC or sports ground campsites out there to keep costs low.\n\nWith a campervan, I recommend splitting the country up into areas you’d like to visit and doing each one as a trip in its own right… unless you’ve got a LOT of time on your hands (like a working holiday visa or a long stay visa).\n\nYou could also break your trip down into a few areas and rent a different campervan out in each one and fly between.\n\nClassic trips include Melbourne to Sydney, Brisbane to Cairns and Adelaide to Darwin.\n\n[> Click Here To BOOK a Deal](https://www.motorhomerepublic.com/?affiliate=roamingrenegades)\n\n![A wicked campervan covered in paint with mountains in the distance in Australia](https://theroamingrenegades.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/australia-travel-tips-campervan.jpg \"16 BEST Australia Travel Tips: What You NEED to Know Before Planning a Trip in 2026! 27\")\n\nWicked campervans come with a bit of a love-hate relationship!  \n*Image:* [The Roaming Renegades](https://www.instagram.com/the_roaming_renegades/)\n\n## The Final Australia Travel Tip: Say G’day to a New Way of Life!\n\nAnnnnd breathe! Ok, I’ve come to the end of this bumper Australia travel tips post, and honestly, it’s got me pumped for another return trip, and I’ve spent a month there already this year!\n\nFor me, Australia is like a second home, and I’ve even picked up a bogan Aussie family along the way, too! It’s just one of those places that keeps calling me back, and the more I explore, the more I realise I’ve still got to see.\n\nFor example, we just spent February in rural NSW on the Murray River with Gav and Jane. An area we’d never been before they moved back up that way. We had the most incredible time fishing, swimming in the river, exploring all the little towns, looking after chooks, and even learning to shoot. It’s a totally different world from what we experienced living in Melbourne or even road tripping through QLD and the outback.\n\nTake it slowly, spend time in the country, get to know the wonderful people that call this place home, explore all the quirky and fascinating nooks and crannies of this Great Southern Land… because I can guarantee you one trip won’t be enough!\n\nLet me know if you have any other useful tips for travelling to Australia.\n\nEnjoy!\n\n![Nic and Shorty with Gav and Jane in Australia ](https://theroamingrenegades.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/nic-shorty-gav-jane-house-australia-tips.jpg \"16 BEST Australia Travel Tips: What You NEED to Know Before Planning a Trip in 2026! 28\")\n\nWith our “Aussie parents” in Howlong, NSW!  \n*Image:* [The Roaming Renegades](https://www.instagram.com/the_roaming_renegades/)\n\n---\n\n### Buy Us a Coffee\n\n[![nic and paul the roaming renegades alhambra spain](https://theroamingrenegades.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/11/nic-and-paul-the-roaming-renegades-alhambra-spain.jpg \"16 BEST Australia Travel Tips: What You NEED to Know Before Planning a Trip in 2026! 29\")](https://buymeacoffee.com/roamingrenegades)\n\nA few people have asked us recently how they could help us out on our travels, so we thought we’d add our very own [tip jar](https://buymeacoffee.com/roamingrenegades) for those who can’t support us by clicking through our affiliate links.\n\nWe work hella hard on this site to bring you all the most epic and up-to-date travel info from around the planet. So if you’ve enjoyed what you’ve seen, then we’d appreciate anything, no matter how small, you can contribute as a thank you.\n\nAbove all, thank you for being here and reading our content, it means the world to us.\n\nNic & Paul\n\n[> Buy Us A Coffee](https://buymeacoffee.com/roamingrenegades)\n\n## Frequently Asked Questions\n\n### \n\nEveryone other than Kiwis needs a visa. They’re simple and easy to get for most countries if you’re planning on staying for 3 months or less. For many countries, they are free (UK, for example), but some will need to pay a $20 admin charge (USA, for example). For longer stays, there are tourist visas available for up to 12 months.\n\n### \n\nSome packing tips for traveling to Australia include: An Australia-specific adapter, good sunscreen, a wide-brimmed hat, lightweight walking pants, a waterproof jacket and a good sense of humour.\n\n### \n\nYes! Don’t worry about all the scary animals, you’re mega unlikely to come across them and with some common sense, it’s easy to stay safe. The biggest things to be aware of are sun and sea safety. Oh, and magpies in spring!\n\n### \n\nHow long do you need in Australia, well that depends on how long you’ve got! Australia needs at least a few months to even scratch the surface as it’s so big. If you’re limited on time then break it into regions and explore one on each trip. I’d recommend at least a month for each visit.\n\n### \n\nMate, it’s incredible! \"Charities\")\n  + [Co-operatives](/co-operatives \"Co-operatives\")\n  + [Street collections](/street-collections \"Street collections\")\n\n \n\n# Grocery unit prices\n\nLast updated: 25 November 2024\n\nUnit pricing at grocery stores shows consumers not just the cost of a product, but what the value of that product is as a cost per standard unit of measurement on shelf labels for groceries. Unit pricing makes it easy to check, compare and save when buying groceries.\n\nLarge grocery stores and some online grocery retailers must display the unit price when selling packaged food and other grocery products, such as bread, eggs, fruit and vegetables and toilet paper.\n\nUse unit pricing to get better value for money by comparing:\n\n* different brands\n* different package sizes and package types\n* special and normal prices\n* packaged and loose – for example spinach\n* fresh, frozen, dried or canned – for example peas\n* similar and substitute products – for example rice types\n* different convenience levels – for example cheese in blocks/wedges/slices/sticks, or grated or diced\n* different grocery retailers, including online stores.\n* unit prices in different parts of the supermarket. The same product may be sold in different sections, for example, cheese, meats, seafood, nuts, fruit and vegetables.\n\nPackaged groceries will often be sold by weight, and liquids sold by volume. For example, you might check and see a 2-kilogram packet of rice for $4.80, with a unit price of $0.24 per 100 grams. You could compare that with a different brand that has 1-kilogram of rice in a box for $3.00, with a unit price of $0.30 per 100grams. Now you can decide which is better value and would suit your situation better.\n\nFor more information on unit pricing and how it can help you save money, visit the [Australian Competition and Consumer Commission](https://www.accc.gov.au/consumers/pricing/unit-prices-for-groceries). .\n\n## Print\n\n## Share\n\n* [(Opens in a new tab/window)](https://www.facebook.com/sharer/sharer.php?u=https://www.consumerprotection.wa.gov.au/grocery-unit-prices \"Facebook\")\n* [(Opens in a new tab/window)](https://x.com/intent/tweet?text=&url=https://www.consumerprotection.wa.gov.au/grocery-unit-prices \"X\")\n* [(Opens in a new tab/window)](https://www.linkedin.com/shareArticle?mini=true&url=https://www.consumerprotection.wa.gov.au/grocery-unit-prices \"LinkedIn\")\n* [(Opens in a new tab/window)](https://www.consumerprotection.wa.gov.au/grocery-unit-prices \"Copy URL to clipboard\")\n\n ",

      "raw_content": "[Skip to content](#content)\n\n[![The Accommodation Brokers Logo](https://theaccommodationbrokers.com.au/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/The-Accommodation-Brokers-Logo.svg) ![The Accommodation Brokers Logo](https://theaccommodationbrokers.com.au/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/The-Accommodation-Brokers-Logo.svg) ![The Accommodation Brokers Logo](https://theaccommodationbrokers.com.au/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/The-Accommodation-Brokers-Logo.svg)](https://theaccommodationbrokers.com.au/)\n\n* ## Travelling – it leaves you speechless, then turns you into a storyteller\n* ## Never get so busy making a living that you forget to make a life\n* ## Never let your memories be greater than your dreams\n* ## You don't need magic to disappear. All you need is a destination\n* ## Once a year, go somewhere you have never been before\n* ## The only trip you will ever regret is the one that you don't take\n\nTRAVEL TIPS[admin](https://theaccommodationbrokers.com.au/author/admin/)2021-10-08T15:53:23+11:00\n\n## Members Travel Tips\n\nNot sure where to travel? Four tips for choosing a travel destination[admin](https://theaccommodationbrokers.com.au/author/admin/)2021-07-06T16:01:31+10:00\n\n#### [Not sure where to travel? Four tips for choosing a travel destination](#collapse-1-15695)\n\n### **Identify the purpose of your trip**\n\nAs previously mentioned, it is important to know what you expect from your holidays before choosing a travel destination. What do you want? Do you want to relax on a deserted beach and leave all your worries behind? If so, there are fashionable destinations like Costa Rica that combine stunning beaches with the power of a volcano. But if you want to find other options, we have some paradisiacal beach destinations for you.\n\nIf, on the other hand, you’re looking for wild experiences when it comes to choosing a travel destination, there are also options for you. Sunrises taken right out of Hollywood, animals in their natural habitat and unnavigable roads are some of the experiences that can be enjoyed in destinations such as Africa. The possibilities are endless; identify what you want to experience and adapt your journey to it.\n\n### **Your time restraints**\n\nThe length of a holiday is another key point when choosing your travel destination. If you have to take a long-haul flight to get there, this deducts two days from the total time you have, one for the outbound journey and another for the return. In addition to the long journey itself, you need time to adapt to the time difference.\n\nOn the other hand, given that these are the places with the longest journey time, it is preferable to opt for them if you have at least two weeks to explore. If your holiday is just seven days, perhaps it would be better to stay in Europe. If you don’t have a set return date, you can take an extra-long trip, even without a return ticket.\n\n### **The size of your budget**\n\nDistance doesn’t always mean a higher price, as it is always possible to find a good offer, wherever your destination. However, it is useful to set a limit on the amount you wish to spend. You must bear in mind that not only will you have to pay for your plane ticket, you also have to think about accommodation, food and the standards of living at the destination.\n\nSome remote areas imply a higher flight price. On the contrary, their currency is worth very little compared to yours. This means that the cost of the tickets can be compensated by lower day-to-day expenses during the holiday. Within Europe, the opposite is often the case; flights can be found at low cost, but accommodation and food costs can be extremely high.\n\n### **What kind of trip you’re looking for**\n\nContinuing on from the previous point, another important point when choosing a travel destination is the type of trip. If you consider yourself an adventurous person, you can let yourself be carried away by the experience and eat in street stalls and other low-budget establishments. Also, when it comes to accommodation, you can share a room with other travellers and get around on foot or rent a bicycle if the terrain permits.\n\nIf travelling comfortably and not having to improvise is more your style, it’s going to cost you. Guided excursions, taxis or dinners in restaurants will considerably raise the budget, but will also mean that you can relax more. Make sure your destination gives you what you’re looking for.\n\nIf Going Overseas Always Refer to the Australian Government “Smart Traveller Website”” for Information[admin](https://theaccommodationbrokers.com.au/author/admin/)2021-07-06T15:58:58+10:00\n\n#### [If Going Overseas Always Refer to the Australian Government “Smart Traveller Website”” for Information](#collapse-1-15699)\n\nSmartraveller website address:  \n https://www.smartraveller.gov.au/\n\nYour Travel Budget[admin](https://theaccommodationbrokers.com.au/author/admin/)2021-07-06T16:04:45+10:00\n\n#### [Your Travel Budget](#collapse-1-15697)\n\nBefore you can even begin to plan a trip, you need to take a good look at your finances and figure out how much money you have to spend on your holiday. This will dictate a lot of the future steps including where you can travel to and for how long.\n\n### **Creating an Initial Budget**\n\n**Determine what you can afford.** Assess how much money you have available for the vacation. Keep in mind your ongoing expenses that you’ll need to take care of when you return like rent, utilities, and food costs. You don’t want to stress yourself out during your vacation by having no money for when you return.\n\n**Get advice from friends and family.** Ask around if anyone you know has visited your destination. While websites and web reviews are helpful, you don’t know if they’ve been influenced by local sponsors or the like. Friends and family will give you more personal and trustworthy advice.\n\n* Ask questions like “What does a meal cost there?” or “What are some cheap things to do there?”\n\n**Use online budgeting tools.** There are numerous websites designed to help your budget specifically for travel. They will help you determine the local costs of goods and what expenses you’ll need to consider.\n\n* Try sites like BudgetYourTrip.com, SavingForTravel.com, and IndepdentTraveler.com. Set up an account and enter the details of your budget and travel expenses.\n\n### **Budgeting for the Basics**\n\n**Determine your method of transportation.** Travel to the location of your choosing may be expensive. Determine the costs of taking a plane, train, coach bus, rental car, or cruise ship to your selected location. Air travel is the quickest option but may be costlier than train, bus, or car rental if the distance isn’t too great. You should also keep in mind the environmental impacts of each method of transportation. A cruise ship affords the greatest luxury and will often include a number of stops but is also the costliest option.\n\n* You can compare plane ticket costs with Google Flights, SkyScanner.com, Expedia, FareCompare.com, or Kayak. Always research price comparisons before making your purchase.\n* **sider local transportation.** Once you reach your destination, you’ll need further transportation to get around locally. Many people take taxi cabs, ride-sharing cars, local transit buses, or the subway to get around locally. If you have some extra money, you can travel more easily by renting a car at your location.\n  + Use your preferred search engine to research public transit at your destination. Not all cities will have all of the options mentioned above.\n  + You can compare rental car prices SkyScanner.com, Expedia, or Kayak as well. Always research price comparisons before making your reservation.\n  + If you are renting a car, you should also consider what rental agencies are close to your airport or hotel.\n\n**Consider lodging expenses.** One of the more significant items you’ll need to budget for is your lodging cost. Lodgings vary greatly in cost and quality so be sure to consider your exact needs and what’s available at your destination. If your destination hosts many tourists, there will likely be a wide variety of hotels, motels, resorts, and bed-and-breakfasts.\n\n* + Pick a hotel that is located near the attractions you’re seeking. This will prove convenient and save you in local travel costs.\n  + Consider amenities like televisions in the rooms, internet access, and access to a swimming pool. You should also consider the quality and size of available beds and bathrooms, the availability of air conditioning, and whether or not they serve a complimentary breakfast. If you have any questions that aren’t answered by their website, call the front desk.\n  + Check customer reviews on Google and Yelp. Keep in mind that nearly every hotel has some excellent reviews and some that are terrible. Read as many as possible to get a comprehensive idea of the quality.\n  + Some locales will have hostels where you can stay at little or no charge in exchange for doing some chores.\n  + You can compare hotel prices and features on Expedia and Kayak as well. You can also use Hotwire, Hotels.com, Priceline, Travelocity, and Agoda. Always research price comparisons before making your reservation because different sites may have different prices at the same hotel.\n\n**Include food costs.** Of course, you’ll need to eat during your trip so you need to budget for meals. Keep in mind that you’ll likely be eating out and that food costs can vary greatly between different places. Use your preferred search engine to determine local food costs.\n\n* + If you need to save some money on food, consider getting a hotel room with a kitchenette or at least a microwave and then purchasing some easy-to-make meals at a local grocery store.\n\n**Keep an incidentals fund.** Always create your travel budget so that there is a little money left over. You’re likely to find some sort of cost that you hadn’t considered beforehand. It could be as simple as needing sunscreen for the beach or pharmaceuticals for an unforeseen illness.\n\n**Consider travel insurance.** Travel insurance is commonly used to insure against a variety of significant unforeseen costs such as medical care that won’t be covered by your insurer because you’re out of network, lost luggage, falling victim to theft, or a transportation accident. Travel insurance can often be purchased from vending machines at airports or online.\n\n* + Allianz, Travel Insurance Direct, CoverMore, Bupa are some websites that offer standalone travel insurance.\n  + You can also get travel insurance from general insurance providers like Geico and State Farm. You may be able to get a discount if you purchase auto, life, or home insurance from these providers already.\n\n### **Budgeting for the Extras**\n\n**Determine sight-seeing costs.** Sight-seeing is a common practice for travelers. Think about the transportation, admittance and other costs related specifically to these trips. Most monuments, parks, and museums are free of charge but some may cost a small amount money. Research these sights beforehand so you can factor them into your budget.\n\n* ook up pre-packaged sight-seeing tours in your destination. They may be the most cost-efficient and thorough way to see a locale’s major sights.\n\n**Determine your entertainment costs.** If you’re planning on attending amusement parks, enjoying the local nightlife, or taking in a show, factor these costs into your budget. You may want to create a rough schedule of your daily entertainment plans so you can research them ahead of time.\n\n* + Use sites like Yelp and TripAdvisor to research local entertainment and get an idea of the costs ahead of time.\n  + Consider getting a AAA membership. They offer travel discounts at restaurants and entertainment venues.\n\n**Consider gifts and souvenirs.** Many travelers purchase gifts for others other souvenirs for themselves. It will be difficult to determine the costs ahead of time so make a budget you can stick to.\n\n* + Make a list of the people you intend to purchase gifts for ahead of time and try to assign a rough dollar amount.\n\n### **Doing Budget-Friendly Planning**\n\n**Save up some money.** Travel can be expensive so developing a comprehensive budget is a great idea.\n\n* You may also need to set aside money from your typical day-to-day expenses so you’ll have enough. Work out a regular amount of money to set aside for your travel expenses and begin saving as soon as possible.\n* If you need some extra money to make your travel budget, consider a part-time or temporary job like driving for a ride-sharing program or writing for an online publication. Search for temporary jobs on websites like Craigslist, Indeed.com, or FlexJobs.com.\n* f you’re a frequent traveler or have travel benefits from your credit card company, you may be able to defray the costs of airfare or travel.\n\n**Convert your currency.** If you are leaving the country, you may need to exchange your money for the local currency. Use your preferred search engine to find the name of the country you’re visiting to determine what type of currency they use. However, many foreign countries that use different currencies also widely accept U.S. Dollars, so you may want to search whether or not this is applicable in your destination.\n\n* + Use the website <http://www.xe.com/currencyconverter/> to determine the exchange rate. Simply enter the amount of money in your travel budget and then change the second box to the currency of your destination country.\n\n**Consider an all-inclusive vacation.** There are a number of agencies that provide all-inclusive vacation packages that can reduce the cost of specific items and make it easier for you to budget. They usually include lodging, food, and entertainment provisions like tickets to amusement parks or guided tours. Specific packages are usually geared toward couples, singles, and families with children.\n\nHow To Choose the Right Type Of Luggage or Bag for your Travels[admin](https://theaccommodationbrokers.com.au/author/admin/)2021-07-06T16:05:27+10:00\n\n#### [How To Choose the Right Type Of Luggage or Bag for your Travels](#collapse-1-15685)\n\n***A JOURNEY OF A THOUSAND MILES BEGINS WITH A TRUSTED TRAVEL BAG. AT EAGLE CREEK, WE BELIEVE ONE OF THE MOST IMPORTANT PARTS OF THAT JOURNEY IS PACKING SMART. THAT’S WHY WE’VE BEEN OBSESSED WITH MAKING DURABLE AND COMPELLING BAGS SINCE THE DAY WE OPENED OUR DOORS. EVEN MORE THOUGH, WE’RE OBSESSED WITH HELPING YOU CHOOSE EXACTLY THE RIGHT LUGGAGE FOR YOUR NEXT TRIP. HERE’S EXACTLY WHAT YOU NEED TO KNOW ABOUT PICKING A WHEELED LUGGAGE VERSUS ROLLING SUITCASES VERSUS DUFFELS, TRAVEL PACKS, AND MORE.***\n\nWe know how hard it can be to squeeze everything you need into one piece of luggage. When you’re cramming everything into that your suitcase, you need the bag itself to have plenty of pockets for organisation, and you also want it to have other smart travel features (like lockable zippers and beefy wheels). After all, we all know the “joy” of sprinting from Gate A3 to Gate Q36 to make a connecting flight. Whether you’re checking your bags or looking for the best lightweight carry-on or travel backpack, we’ve got the solution for you. This handy buying guide will help you choose the right type of luggage for your journey.\n\nWhether you’re a frequent jet setter or an occasional traveller, you don’t want to get stuck with bulky, poor-quality travel bags that get in the way of your trip. Take the time to think about the needs of your trip, and choose your bags and packing organisers accordingly. Knowing what to expect—and how much you’ll need to pack—will enable you to easily choose between different travel packs and duffels, as well as individual features such as wheels, handles, sizes, and organisational travel accessories.\n\n### **WHAT IS THE BEST LUGGAGE FOR YOUR TRAVELS?**\n\nTo ensure that you choose luggage, suitcases, and travel bags that are a perfect fit for your needs, here are a few important things to consider.\n\n1. **Length of journey**. How long will you be traveling? For a weekend trip, you may be able to fit everything into a lightweight carry-on. For a longer adventure, you’ll want to consider a piece of rolling luggage depending what type of gear you’ll need to bring.\n2. **Modes of transportation**. Will you have multiple layovers or include budget flights? Will your journey include train or bus rides? If you’ll be on the go and moving between multiple types of transportation, you’ll absolutely want a lightweight carry-on, wheeled backpack, or even a backpack duffel that’s easy to handle and fits in overhead compartments of trains, planes, and buses.\n3. **Type of travel**. Will you be camping in remote locations or staying at a posh hotel? Depending on where and how you’re traveling, the amount and type of gear you’ll need may vary. A traveler on the go will be looking for the lightest travel pack possible, while those staying in a hotel or hostel will be able to more easily consider a piece of rolling luggage.\n4. **Activities**. What type of activities will you be doing and what do you need to pack to do them? If you’ll be laying on a beach and plan on packing bathing suits and sarongs, your suitcase needs will likely be much different than someone who will be packing climbing gear and using multiple modes of transportation to get there. Some situations call for an adventurous bag capable of holding up to mud, rain, and being strapped to the roof of a bus, while other in situations you’ll be glad for a versatile bag with a separate wet compartment to hold swimsuits and beach gear.\n5. **Research**. Check out packing organisation tips on Travel Bloggers Blogs to get ideas of exactly what to bring with you on your next trip!\n\nThere’s a correct piece of luggage for every type of trip. Whether you’re shopping for one piece or an entire collection, you can make your travel so much easier when you are well-equipped. So now that you know your travel needs, you’re ready to choose the perfect travel bag. We’ve broken each type of bag down by category and recommended use.\n\n### **LIGHTWEIGHT CARRY-ONS**\n\n***Recommended use****: International travel, weekend trips, overnight stays, or single-day business trips*\n\nMost people try to maximize their carry-on packing, fitting everything they can into the luggage dimensions allowed by the airline. This is the way to go when traveling (if you can do it) because it’s really nice to know your bag will be arriving at your destination with you. Purchase lightweight carry-ons that offer all the features you love—retractable handles, durable wheels, multiple compartments for organisation, and more— make sure they are in compact sizes that are light, super easy to carry, and designed specifically to fit in the overhead bin (without cramming and slamming).\n\n### **ROLLING LUGGAGE**\n\n***Recommended use****: Use rolling luggage for business travel, weekend trips, and well… most of the time*.\n\nThe tried and true favourites of most seasoned travellers are large rolling bags. Gone are the days of lugging a massive suitcase by a single handle. Now you have a variety of rolling luggage to choose from to carry your heavy belongings with ease.\n\nMake sure you’re focused on quality when choosing one of these handy travel mates as wheels can break and sometimes get stuck. Large rolling bags or wheeled duffels are a great option if you need a lot of space—the spacious main compartment allows you to fit a ton of gear, which is easily organised once you understand how to use packing cubes. But for those who’d like a little more organisation in their luggage, a wheeled upright typically comes with more compartments to separate your goods. You may also want to consider convertible luggage, which offer the convenience of wheels, backpack straps, retractable handles and so much more.\n\nIt’s also a good idea to think about whether you want your rolling luggage to have the traditional two wheels or four. Many people enjoy having 4-wheeled luggage because the bag glides almost effortlessly by your side, easily rolling down the aisle of the plane. Four wheels also makes travel less strenuous because you’re not putting a ton of weight on your wrists. Plus, a 4-wheeled bag gives you a little more versatility—for example, if you’re pulling your bag up a curb, simply tilt the bag back and pull it on two wheels. However, one thing to note about 4-wheeled luggage is if you are doing lots of travel by bus, and will need to store your bag in an upright position, you may want to opt for 2-wheeled luggage, because 4-wheeled bags can move around easily on buses in motion.\n\n### **BACKPACKS AND WHEELED BACKPACKS**\n\n***Recommended use****: Day trips, adventure travel, multi-destination, and international travel*\n\nRolling uprights are a great option for carrying lots of gear, but depending on where you’re going, you may find it more comfortable and convenient to carry a travel backpack or backpack duffel instead. If you want to merge the concept of travel backpack and rolling bag, consider a convertible backpack which converts from one into the other. Whichever bag you decide to travel with, you may be surprised at how light today’s packs are when you carry them on your back—instead of having to constant roll them behind you.\n\n### **TRAVEL PACKS AND DUFFELS**\n\n***Recommended use****: Business travel, day trips, round the world trips, and adventure travel*\n\nA travel pack is a great alternative to traditional piece of luggage or suitcase. You may find that it offers versatility that many other bags don’t. When packing for any kind of trip, remember that you don’t always want to lug around a giant rolling upright behind you. Travel backpacks are great for folks that plan to be on the go a lot and may face the challenge of cobblestone and dirt streets. And travel duffels work well for adventure travel—the bathtub construction and water repellent fabric are a great boon on certain types of trips.\n\nShould I get Travel Insurance?[admin](https://theaccommodationbrokers.com.au/author/admin/)2021-07-06T16:08:33+10:00\n\n#### [Should I get Travel Insurance?](#collapse-1-15663)\n\n**Travel insurance**\n\nTravel doesn’t always go as planned. If you’re going overseas, travel insurance is as important as a [passport](https://www.smartraveller.gov.au/consular-services/passport-services). Without it, you or your family could suffer financially if things go wrong. No matter who you are, where you’re going and what you’re doing, get insurance.\n\nSome travel insurance policies internationally may cover COVID-19-related claims. These policies aren’t widely available in Australia yet. Some travel insurers are starting to sell international travel insurance to Australians. However, it may not cover COVID-19-related claims.\n\nA ban on overseas travel from Australia remains in place. You can’t leave Australia unless you get an [exemption from the Department of Home Affairs.](https://covid19.homeaffairs.gov.au/leaving-australia)\n\nMost standard policies also won’t cover you for ‘Do not travel’ destinations. Check with your travel insurance provider.\n\nFor more information about international travel insurance see the CHOICE website: [Does travel insurance cover the COVID-19 coronavirus?
