Use removable zip ties to close the crate securely; the last thing you want is for your pet to break free and get into the cargo hold, where the risk of injury is significant.\n* **Freeze a small bowl of water and place it inside the crate.** The ice won’t spill during loading, but it’ll be drinkable as it defrosts during the flight. If you’ve got a layover and someone else will need to feed your pet enroute, put the pet food in a plastic bag and secure it to the outside of the crate along with feeding instructions—and attach an empty food bowl inside the crate.\n* Similar to train travel, **don’t overfeed your pet before flying**. Give your animal a light meal several hours before take off to avoid nausea during the flight. And if you can, walk your dog before the journey to help him expend some energy pre-boarding.\n* **Don’t sedate your pet.** “Sedatives during air travel can increase the risk of heart or respiratory issues potentially caused by changing altitudes and atmospheric pressures,” says Kurt Venator, DVM, PhD, Purina’s chief veterinary officer. “Sedatives may also interfere with your pet’s balance or equilibrium while being transported in a carrier or crate.”\n* When you board, **tell the flight attendants and pilots that your pet is in cargo** so they can be extra mindful of the temperature and air pressure there.\n* **Don’t be shy; advocate for your pet.** Ask airline staff about her status as soon as you land.\n\nPut your room number and hotel address in your phone[admin](https://theaccommodationbrokers.com.au/author/admin/)2021-07-09T10:33:33+10:00\n\n#### [Put your room number and hotel address in your phone](#collapse-1-15766)\n\nAm I the only one who can’t remember my hotel room number and the address of the place I am staying?\n\nPut both these details in your phone when you arrival and delete when you leave – simple – saves a lot of hassle!\n\n5 rules to follow when using free Wi-Fi overseas[admin](https://theaccommodationbrokers.com.au/author/admin/)2021-07-09T10:33:07+10:00\n\n#### [5 rules to follow when using free Wi-Fi overseas](#collapse-1-15768)\n\nWhether you’re looking for restaurant recommendations or trying to figure out where your hotel is, free Wi-Fi can be an absolute godsend when you’re travelling.\n\nBut this convenience also comes with a degree of risk.\n\nPublic Wi-Fi networks are notorious for security flaws that put personal data at risk, if you haven’t taken the necessary precautions. Here are five rules for connecting to Wi-Fi overseas. Follow these rules and you’ll be able to get online safely and securely.\n\n**1. Customise your phone’s security setup**\n\nWe forget that our portable devices are just as vulnerable to malicious software as our computers, so consider purchasing security software for your phone before travelling.\n\n**2. Use strong, long passwords**\n\nA lot goes into a password, but it pays to make them complicated. Longer, more-complicated passwords that are unique to different accounts are much more difficult to hack and provide another level of protection when using your devices.\n\n**3. Make sure the network is legitimate**\n\nThis is one of the most common ways hackers trick travellers. Before connecting to a network at a hotel of café, double check with the staff or manager the name of the network to make sure you’re not connecting to a dummy, insecure alternative.\n\n**4. Consider using a virtual private network (VPN)**\n\nEven if the network you’re using is password-protected, there’s still a chance your communication could be intercepted. Well, okay \\*maybe\\* the plague would get a look in, but excess baggage fees would be a close second.\n\n### What are excess baggage fees?\n\nExcess baggage fees are charges that you incur if your bags exceed the dimensions or weight allowances set forth by the airlines.\n\n### How to avoid excess baggage fees\n\nThere are lots of ways to ensure you won’t get charged those pesky excess baggage fees – but don’t worry, you won’t have to wear your entire wardrobe. From choosing a lightweight bag, cracking out the scales, or sharing packing space, here are our top tips for avoiding additional fees.\n\n### 1. Pay for extra bags online and in advance\n\nIf you know you’re going to go over the weight or size limit, or are worried about it, it’s almost always cheaper to book extra luggage allowances in advance. You’ll find that most airlines will offer discounts of up to 50% if you pay online instead of choking up airport queues. Often you can pay for extra baggage by the kilo, or by piece.\n\nBudget carriers like Jetstar and Tigerair have baggage allowances which start at around $36, so it’s absolutely worth scaling up if you’re unsure of how much you’re bringing, so you can save on those hefty baggage fees later.\n\n### 2. Weigh your bags at home\n\nIt may sound obvious to weigh your bags before you leave, but so many people rely on the ol’ pick-it-up-and-guess trick, and if you’re off by a couple of kilos, it can hit your wallet where it hurts. Double check the weight of your bag once you’ve packed, and if you’re over, you can take out a few things.\n\nHowever, trying to weigh your bag on bathroom scales is harder than being an acrobat in *Cirque du Soleil*, so we recommend portable luggage scales. These cheap, handy tools are also small and easy to pop in your bag, especially useful if you’re the kind of traveller that loves to shop. These magic little gadgets will save you having to deal with baggage fees on the return journey.\n\n### 3. Share ~~the love~~ baggage space\n\nIf you’re at the check-in desk, and horror of horrors, your bag is terribly overweight, you can fall on the mercy of a travelling partner – especially if they’re a light packer. Swap a few things around and even out the load between your bags. Most airline staff will allow you to do it near the desk, but you can always pop to the side and quickly sort out your bags if you’re worried about holding up the line.\n\nIf you’re a planner, and the thought of a last minute pack-fest is not your idea of a good time, airlines like Jetstar let you buy your baggage by kilos, so you can purchase up to 40kg, and spread it out over a couple of bags. In this way, it won’t matter if the two bags are weighted unevenly, as long as they don’t exceed the total limit.\n\n### 4. Buy lightweight luggage\n\nNo one ever thinks of the weight of the actual bags, and some options can weight up to 5kg – empty! Lightweight and durable baggage options will allow for all those extra souvenirs you just *had* to buy, whilst not racking up annoying baggage fees.\n\nOlder suitcase models can have heavy frames, which will eat up your weight allowance, so definitely check out what new lightweight models are available.\n\n### How much will I be charged if my bags exceed the weight or size limits?\n\nExcess charges vary by airline. To help you out we’ve put together a handy list you can crosscheck your airline to know exactly how much you could be charged.\n\n| Airline | Excess baggage charge |\n| --- | --- |\n| Air Canada | $100CAD ($107) for an overweight bag, $225CAD ($240) for an additional checked bag. |\n| Air China | 190-700CNY ($38-142) for excess within allowed pieces, additional pieces start at 700CNY ($142). |\n| Air New Zealand | $35-205NZD ($32-187) per bag – please note these are pre-paid values. |\n| American Airlines | $100-$200USD ($139-278) per bag |\n| ANA | $40-140 depending on whether it is an extra piece or overweight. |\n| China Eastern | 1000CNY ($203) for the first piece, 2000CNY ($406) for the second |\n| China Southern | 1000CNY ($203) for the first piece, 2000CNY ($406) for the second |\n| Emirates | From $40USD ($55) per kg |\n| Etihad Airways | From $70USD ($98) per every 2kg |\n| Fiji Airways | From $18FJD ($12) per kg |\n| Jetstar | From $15 per kg |\n| KLM | €55-100 ($90-163) per bag depending on route and travel class |\n| Korean Air | From 70000KRW ($87) per piece |\n| Qantas | $78 per extra piece on domestic routes, and from $20 per kg on international routes. |\n| Rex Airlines | $7.70 per extra kg or $16.50 per oversized piece + $7.70 for excess weight |\n| Tigerair | From $20 per kg |\n| United | From $100USD ($139) per piece |\n| Vietnam Airlines | From $10USD ($14) per kg |\n| Virgin Australia | From $70 per piece |\n\n### The above prices are a guide – please check with the airline you are flying with to get the correct pricing.\n\n### Note:\n\nSome oversized or overweight baggage can be classed as cargo and subject to additional fees if you’ve exceeded the airline’s maximum weight restrictions. Excess baggage fees vary according to route and/or destination. Typically an overweight bag is classed between 23-32kg on long haul flights.\n\nTalk to the Locals[admin](https://theaccommodationbrokers.com.au/author/admin/)2021-07-09T11:16:38+10:00\n\n#### [Talk to the Locals](#collapse-1-15776)\n\n### Why you should try and meet locals while traveling\n\nWhen you travel abroad, you can follow your itinerary, stay inside your bubble and keep your conversations limited to your travel companions. Or, you can branch out and meet locals while traveling. It’s more comfortable to stay with what you know. But in order to get the most out of your travel experience, you might need to stretch yourself. Strike up conversations wherever you go. The rewards are immense.\n\n### Top 5 Reasons to Meet Locals While Traveling\n\n#### 1. Out of comfort zone\n\nTravel is all about getting out of your comfort zone: new foods, new places, unexpected delays, and language barriers. Meeting new people while traveling is yet one more way to stretch yourself. Why do we hesitate to put ourselves out there? Fear of rejection, awkwardness, or simply being unsure how to begin a conversation: these are some of the top reasons we avoid meeting new people. Like any other skill, striking up a conversation with a stranger is something you will feel more comfortable doing the more often you try. Stepping out of your comfort zone in this way is so important for building your confidence and people skills.\n\n#### 2. Cultural Immersion\n\nIf you really want to get immersed in culture and language, there is no better way than to meet locals while traveling. You will learn more from talking to real people than you ever will from a guidebook or even the internet. The best way to learn is by asking great questions. But remember, your destination is not just “your destination.” It is someone’s home. Be a respectful, curious, engaged listener wherever you go.\n\n#### 3. Authentic experience\n\nDo you want to know the best places to get tapas in Granada or the best place to watch the sunset along the Seine? Talk to a local! The right person can point you to the food, sights, and experiences that the tourists don’t know about.\n\n#### 4. New opportunities\n\n> If you want to see the world in a way you never have, you will have to do something you’ve never done.\n\nMaking friends while traveling abroad is a great way to open doors of opportunity. This is especially important if you’re traveling solo with the intent to have a more unique, personal experience. By stepping out and meeting new people, you might find yourself with opportunities you wouldn’t have if you kept to yourself. Perhaps it’s an invitation to someone’s home, a family party, or even a simple tour around town. If you want to see the world in a way you never have, you will have to do something you’ve never done.\n\n#### 5. Lifelong friendships\n\nIf you have the opportunity to form a really meaningful connection with someone while abroad, you could very well find yourself with a lifelong friendship. You might even find yourself inviting your new friends to visit you at home, or with an invitation to return to theirs (with somewhere free to stay). Overcome your nerves and strike up a conversation — it will be worth it!\n\n### How to meet people while traveling\n\n#### 1. Start a conversation\n\nAt coffee shops, in restaurants, parks, and on public transit… The best way to meet locals while traveling is to simply start a conversation.\n\n#### 2. Work or volunteer\n\nIf you plan to go abroad for a longer stretch of time, do some volunteering or pick up a part-time job. Working with other people is one of the best ways to connect with them.\n\n#### 3. Stay with locals\n\nAre you interested in trying something besides a traditional hotel for your accommodations? Try Couchsurfing. If you find an Airbnb option to rent out just a room of a home (rather than the whole house), there’s a good chance you’ll be able to connect with your host.\n\n#### 4. Friend of a friend\n\nGet the word out that you will be traveling abroad. Using your Facebook, Instagram, or other network channels, you can say something like, “Hey, friends! I’ll be traveling to Japan this summer. Does anyone have friends or family I could meet while I’m there?” Be sure to use your discretion when sharing specifics about your trip online.\n\n#### 5. Use an app\n\nThere are many great apps such as MeetUp and Showaround to help connect you with people who share your interests.\n\nDon’t be afraid to meet new people, both locals and other travelers, as you travel abroad. With so many great booking platforms online, you’re in the best position to find the exact accommodation or travel experience you want.\n\n### What we do (and do really well)\n\nOnce you’ve found the **exact product you want**, we step in.\n\nUsing our **exclusive booking channels — many not available to the general public — we work to secure you a better price for that same product.**\n\nThink of it as **price improvement**, not product searching.\n\n---\n\n## How to Get Started\n\n### 1️⃣ Choose your destination or travel experience\n\nDecide where you want to go or what type of trip you’d like to take.\n\n### 2️⃣ Select your travel dates\n\nNote your **check-in and check-out dates** (or departure and return dates).\n\n### 3️⃣ Find your product and price\n\nSearch online and choose the **exact accommodation or travel product** you want.  \nMake sure you note:\n\n* The **price**\n* The **room or product type**\n* The **terms and conditions**\n\n### 4️⃣ Send us the details\n\nOnce you’ve found everything, simply submit the information so we can try to beat the price.\n\nYou can send it to us in either of these easy ways:\n\n📧 **Email:** bookings@theaccommodationbrokers.com.au  \n📝 **Online Form:** Complete the form below with your details\n\n---\n\n💡 **Tip:** The more information you provide, the better!  \nWe can only improve the price when we’re comparing the **exact same product — apples with apples.**\n\n---\n\n## What Happens Next?\n\nOnce we receive your details, our team will get to work straight away.\n\nWe’ll check our exclusive booking channels and **come back to you as soon as possible with our best available price.**\n\n---\n\n✨ We look forward to helping you **save money on your next trip!**\n\n### **Welcome to your members** Major Events Accommodation Offers\n\n### It is very simple to get the best market rate\n\n### **View the Product or Destination**\n\n### Click the ask for a quote now button\n\n### Fill out the form with the required information and send\n\n### The Accommodation Brokers will come back to you with a quote for that particular product\n\n### Your members discount will be applied to the quote.\n\n### If you have any questions or the product you wish to purchase is not available please email us at bookings@theaccommodationbrokers.com.au.\n\n### Remember **“Memories Last Forever”**\n\n### The Accommodation Brokers Team\n\nHow to pay by EFT\n\nTo pay by EFT, please deposit the product’s EFT price into the following banking account  \n with these details:\n\n|  |  |\n| --- | --- |\n| Bank name | ANZ |\n| Account name | The Accommodation Brokers |\n| BSB | 012 295 |\n| Account | 472 159 378 |\n| Swift Code | ANZBAU3M |\n\nPlease email us a copy of your remittance at  \n [bookings@theaccommodationbrokers.com.au](mailto:bookings@theaccommodationbrokers.com.au).\n\nLogin\n\n[Go to Top](#)\n\n ",

dark\n* Follow system settings\n\n* [ABC iView](https://iview.abc.net.au)\n* [ABC Listen](https://www.abc.net.au/listen)\n\n[ABC News](/)\n\n[News Home](/news)\n\nHow do Australia's grocery prices compare to the UK, Ireland and New Zealand?\n\n# How do Australia's grocery prices compare to the UK, Ireland and New Zealand?\n\nBy families reporter [Fiona Blackwood](/news/fiona-blackwood/10364982)\n\n* [Topic:Cost of Living](/news/topic/cost-of-living)\n\nPosted , updated\n\n![A collection of groceries inlcuding apples. bananas, milk and mince](https://live-production.wcms.abc-cdn.net.au/48b8008f60806f08638511967eb3fc1d?impolicy=wcms_crop_resize&cropH=2813&cropW=5000&xPos=0&yPos=260&width=862&height=485)\n\nTesco and Sainsbury's in the UK were part of the price comparison.(ABC News: Adrian Wilson)\n\n## In short:\n\nResearchers have compared the prices of common grocery items between leading supermarkets in Australia, the UK, Ireland and New Zealand.\n\nWhen it comes to the overall cost of a basket of groceries, Australia is third most expensive, behind New Zealand, but is second cheapest when the average wages of workers is factored in.\n\n## What's next?\n\nThe study comes amid inquiries and legal action against the big supermarkets in Australia; whether that will translate to cheaper prices remains to be seen.\n\nWe all know the cost of groceries has gone up in Australia.\n\nBut would your shopping be cheaper in comparable countries like New Zealand, the UK or Ireland?\n\n![A shopfront with flowers for sale](https://live-production.wcms.abc-cdn.net.au/48e7faab29257c93dc9c2fc5bdc32ebf?impolicy=wcms_crop_resize&cropH=4000&cropW=6000&xPos=0&yPos=0&width=862&height=575)\n\nSainsbury's is one of the popular supermarket chains in the UK.(ABC News: Adrian Wilson)\n\nNow, you can see for yourself.\n\nResearchers from Edith Cowan University have collected and compared the prices of some common supermarket staples.\n\nHere's how Australia's duopoly performs compared to other leading supermarket brands overseas — Sainsbury's, Tesco, Pak'n'Save, Countdown and Dunnes.\n\nAssociate Professor Flavio Macau and Dr Alex Wang collected data on 44 grocery items between April and May this year.\n\nThe above table shows a sample of their findings.\n\nThey wanted to check how Australia stacks up to similar markets overseas and whether the Coles and Woolworths duopoly is to blame for high grocery prices.\n\n> \"If the situation is a lot better elsewhere, Australia should learn from other countries and take the necessary steps to change its market,\"\n\n Dr Macau said.\n\n![A shopfront with flowers for sale](https://live-production.wcms.abc-cdn.net.au/1419744108094155082119beafa29ba8?impolicy=wcms_crop_resize&cropH=2688&cropW=4032&xPos=0&yPos=168&width=862&height=575)\n\nThe UK was slightly cheaper than Australia for milk. New Zealand fared far worse though.(ABC News: Adrian Wilson)\n\n## How does Australia compare?\n\nFirst of all, let's look at the cost of groceries in Australia.\n\nFood prices at Coles and Woolworths [rose by 9.6 per cent over the past 12 months to April.](https://102380456)\n\nBut the price difference between the two major supermarkets is small.\n\n![Colourful tins, jars and boxes on a kitchen pantry shelf.](https://live-production.wcms.abc-cdn.net.au/99424e91e3a0b4252e048a0e06e70984?impolicy=wcms_crop_resize&cropH=4632&cropW=6948&xPos=0&yPos=0&width=862&height=575)\n\nThe study found a standard basket of groceries in Australia is less expensive than New Zealand.(ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)\n\nDr Macau found in a grocery trolley of 50 products, the cost of 45 products was the same at Woolworths and Coles.\n\nThe overall price difference on a $300 shop was less than a dollar.\n\n![Fruit and vegetables on supermarket shelves](https://live-production.wcms.abc-cdn.net.au/e21cd8100fa85cc9572a0d055722371d?impolicy=wcms_crop_resize&cropH=2309&cropW=3463&xPos=0&yPos=296&width=862&height=575)\n\nThe UK's two leading supermarkets generally had a bigger difference in price between them than Coles and Woolworths in Australia.(ABC News: Adrian Wilson)\n\nYet Choice [found an Aldi trolley of groceries was 25 per cent cheaper.](/news/2024-06-20/choice-supermarket-prices-report-coles-woolworths-aldi-iga/103997340)\n\n> \"While we do not go as far as to say that Woolworths and Coles control prices, they possibly monitor each other's moves very closely,\"\n\n Dr Macau said.\n\nThis could mean the big supermarkets are either in a battle to the bottom on price or a cruise to the top.\n\n\"To better understand what's happening in Australia, we compared it with overseas markets,\" Dr Wang said.\n\n## Is there more competition overseas?\n\n![Customers walk past the entrance to a supermarket.](https://live-production.wcms.abc-cdn.net.au/4bd55173cabb2ab71a2cc6c7c210bc8b?impolicy=wcms_crop_resize&cropH=2726&cropW=4089&xPos=456&yPos=0&width=862&height=575)\n\nIn the UK, Tesco and Sainsbury's account for 42 per cent of the market.(ABC News: Adrian Wilson)\n\nThe comparison looked at the two largest supermarkets in each country, to mimic Australia's Coles-Woolworths duopoly, which has 65 per cent of the market share.\n\nIn New Zealand, there's a similar duopoly — Pak'n'Save and Countdown (New Zealand's brand for Woolworths) hold 70 per cent of the market.\n\nIn the UK, Tescos and Sainsbury's account for 42 per cent of the market.\n\nWhile in Ireland, Dunnes and Tescos hold a 45 per cent share.\n\n![packaged meat](https://live-production.wcms.abc-cdn.net.au/2e6aaeab80009681203ffa0bf6c6ffc8?impolicy=wcms_crop_resize&cropH=2529&cropW=3794&xPos=0&yPos=159&width=862&height=575)\n\nThe study compared the price of common grocery items.(ABC News: Adrian Wilson)\n\nDr Macau found prices varied significantly more overseas between supermarkets compared to Australia.\n\n> \"While differing prices suggest more choice for consumers, this alone does not confirm that Australians are worse off,\"\n\n he said.\n\n## Which country is the winner?\n\nTo make a fair comparison Dr Macau and Dr Wang found unit prices for each grocery item and applied exchange rates to have all prices listed in Australian dollars and added up the cost of a trolley full of groceries.\n\nThe total cost of the so-called \"basket\" of groceries (language used by the researchers but in actual fact more like a trolley full) is the sum of all 44 grocery items tracked in the research.\n\nHere's the winning order on price alone:\n\n* **UK** — on top with the lowest prices, with the cost of the groceries ranging between **$283—$297**.\n* **Ireland** — next cheapest with prices ranging between **$313—$345**.\n* **Australia** — in third with the price the groceries between **$324—$332**.\n* **New Zealand** — the most expensive with a cost ranging from **$342—$409**.\n\n![A graphic of a shopping basket and price dockets behind it.](https://live-production.wcms.abc-cdn.net.au/301ae2391983dd49b5c1bb25d03f95ed?impolicy=wcms_crop_resize&cropH=1547&cropW=2321&xPos=252&yPos=277&width=862&height=575)\n\nThe UK came out on top.(ABC News: Paul Yeomans)\n\nBut, that's not quite the full story. The average wages of workers are different between the countries.\n\nDr Macau and Dr Wang compared the prices to wages, calculating how many hours a typical person would need to work to buy the trolley load of groceries.\n\n> \"Ireland does not hold second place if we consider wages. In Ireland, you need to work an additional one to two hours to afford the same basket of goods in Australia,\"\n\n Dr Macau said.\n\n![Supermarket shelves lined with juice](https://live-production.wcms.abc-cdn.net.au/45185b91d767082061556b8daac2a273?impolicy=wcms_crop_resize&cropH=2675&cropW=4013&xPos=0&yPos=167&width=862&height=575)\n\nThe UK beat the others for the lowest prices, the study found.(ABC News: Adrian Wilson)\n\nWhen adjusting for wages, **Australia's grocery \"basket\" is the second cheapest:**\n\n* UK\n* **Australia**\n* Ireland\n* New Zeland\n\nDr Macau said, based on median incomes, both Australian and UK shoppers spent about 13 per cent of their wages on groceries, which includes food and non-food items.\n\n> \"This data illustrates that while supermarket checkout prices are a genuine concern, Australians are not alone in facing the issue — similar countries are experiencing comparable struggles,\"\n\n he said.\n\n## Action taken against Australia's supermarket duopoly\n\n[Coles recently posted a $1.1 billion profit for the 2023-24 financial year](/news/2024-08-27/asx-markets-business-news-live-updates/104272052), up 2.1 per cent on the previous year.\n\n[While Woolworths experienced a 93 per cent drop in profit to $108 million](/news/2024-08-28/asx-markets-business-news-live-updates-28-august/104277086), partly due to its operations in New Zealand.\n\n![Colourful tins, jars and boxes on a kitchen pantry shelf.](https://live-production.wcms.abc-cdn.net.au/09dd95d5aa930af90c8444d7e3cf4997?impolicy=wcms_crop_resize&cropH=4501&cropW=6751&xPos=139&yPos=159&width=862&height=575)\n\nMultiple inquiries are currently underway into the supermarket set up in Australia.(ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)\n\nMultiple inquiries [are underway into the supermarket set-up in Australia.](/news/2024-08-21/supermarket-inquiries-impact-on-customers-grocery-bills/104246438)\n\n[Australia's competition watchdog has launched legal action against Coles and Woolworths](/news/2024-09-23/accc-taking-court-action-woolworths-coles-/104383468), accusing them of increasing prices on products only to later advertise them as discounted.\n\nColes says it takes compliance with Australian consumer law extremely seriously and intends to defend the proceedings, while Woolworths says it will review the claims and continue to engage with the consumer watchdog.\n\n## Researchers suggest breaking up the duopoly might be 'counterproductive'\n\n![A man wearing a black puffer jacket and light blue collared business shirt with a sandstone building in the distance.](https://live-production.wcms.abc-cdn.net.au/262924d7af35750f2ddd038c9f2943a0?impolicy=wcms_crop_resize&cropH=3333&cropW=5000&xPos=0&yPos=0&width=862&height=575)\n\nTasmanian senator Nick McKim says Australia's supermarket duopoly needs to be broken up.(ABC News: Sebastian Baltyn)\n\nThe federal Greens are calling for the supermarket duopoly to be broken up.\n\n\"Coles' $1.1 billion profit is a sick joke for the millions of Australians struggling to afford food and groceries,\" Greens senator Nick McKim said.\n\n> \"They are price gouging as food prices continue to drive Australia's stubbornly high inflation numbers.\"\n\nBut Dr Macau said his study pointed to the need for a more nuanced approach.\n\n\"Implementing radical solutions, such as compelling supermarkets to disinvest, might have counterproductive effects, potentially increasing prices due to rising costs,\" he said.\n\n![A man in a suit smiles, with his arms crossed](https://live-production.wcms.abc-cdn.net.au/1c84a0b4e886864ef2f40e52c5aa0e3b?impolicy=wcms_crop_resize&cropH=1365&cropW=2048&xPos=0&yPos=0&width=862&height=575)\n\nAssociate Professor Flavio Macau says there is no magical fix for bringing down prices at the checkout.(Supplied: Edith Cowan University)\n\nHe said despite the perception that supermarket profits were substantial, they were modest when examined through the context of costs and revenue.\n\nDr Macau compared the supermarkets' earnings before interest and taxes divided by sales for 2024.\n\nHe found Coles to be 4.8 per cent, Woolworths 4.7 per cent, Pak'n'Save was 2.6 per cent, Countdown 1.3 per cent and Tescos 7.1 per cent after a difficult year the previous year.\n\n![A man in a plaid shirt wearing glasses](https://live-production.wcms.abc-cdn.net.au/defbef2badb5ab7d1ca0881110d47dc7?impolicy=wcms_crop_resize&cropH=1365&cropW=2048&xPos=0&yPos=0&width=862&height=575)\n\nDr Alex Wang was part of the team who evaluated the price of groceries across the four countries.(Supplied: Edith Cowan University)\n\nDr Macau said ACCC investigations into allegations of consumer deception by Coles and Woolworths highlight that accountability was key.\n\n> \"However, vilifying them is not a fix for the cost-of-living crisis,\"\n\n he said.\n\n\"A strategy that empowers consumers with smart shopping practices and encourages strategic purchasing could offer a more immediate and effective solution.\"\n\nLoading...",

      "raw_content": "Inquiry into food pricing and food security in remote Indigenous communities Submission 36 - Supplementary Submission Food prices and accessibility in remote communities: simple ‘basket of goods’ snapshot July 2020 Inquiry into food pricing and food security in remote Indigenous communities Submission 36 - Supplementary Submission Summary: Food prices and accessibility in remote communities Community stores operate in the some of the most remote areas of Australia. This simple ‘basket of goods’ snapshot provides current pricing (May and June 2020) and draws on more comprehensive surveys such as the NT Government’s Market Basket Survey 2019 and WA Regional Price Index 2019. In consultation with five managed store companies engaged on the NIAA Food Security Working Group – Outback Stores, Community Enterprises Queensland, Mai Wiru, TAH Northern Trading, and the Arnhem Land Progress Aboriginal Corporation – the snapshot analysis covers 47 participating community stores in remote and very remote communities across Queensland, the Northern Territory, South Australia and Western Australia. The participating managed store locations makes up around 22 per cent of the estimated 217 community stores operating across Australia.\nThe average price across the 47 remote stores was around 39 per cent higher when compared with major supermarkets in capital cities. When compared to a limited selection of smaller supermarkets in remote town centres, average community store prices ranged considerably − from 37 per cent higher in South Australia to 16 per cent lower in Western Australia − highlighting the importance of a range of factors to prices across remote communities. The previous parliamentary inquiry into ‘food stores servicing remote Indigenous communities’ and a 2014 study into food pricing and quality in Western Australia noted food prices were higher in remote communities due to a range of factors including: transport costs (fuel, mode of transport, weather, road conditions), the requirement for adequate storage (particularly in locations where the wet season restricts access), store manager wages and housing needs (electricity and bills), repairing and maintaining infrastructure (e.g. freezers and air conditioners) and store management practices (HoRSCIA 2009, Pollard et al 2014, Pollard, 2013). The snapshot provides a summary of prices in select stores. It is not intended as a comprehensive survey. Due to travel restrictions during COVID-19, the information presented has been provided by five managed store companies based on available pricing data and could not be externally validated. NIAA | Basket of goods report 2 NIAA | Food prices and accessibility in remote communities: snapshot July 2020 Inquiry into food pricing and food security in remote Indigenous communities Submission 36 - Supplementary Submission NIAA | Food prices and accessibility in remote communities: snapshot July 2020 3 In the Northern Territory food prices were higher in remote communities compared with district centres In 2019, the NT Market Basket Survey surveyed 58 stores across the Darwin, East Arnhem, Katherine and Alice Springs districts. Prices were collected for two different baskets of goods for a family of six over a fortnight.\n• A Healthy Food Basket consists of food recommended in the Australian Guide to Healthy Eating.\n• A Current Diet Basket was based on the dietary patterns of Indigenous Australians.\nOn average, a Healthy Food Basket in remote community stores was 56 per cent more expensive than major supermarkets in the district centre, and 6 per cent higher than corner stores in the district centre. On average, a Current Diet Basket in remote community stores was 40 per cent more expensive than major supermarkets, and 8 per cent higher than corner stores in the district centre. Sources: Hugo Centre for Population and Housing (2006); Northern Territory Government (2020).\nDarwin Major supermarket Healthy Food Basket: $517 Current Diet Basket: $672 District remote store average Healthy Food Basket: $832 Current Diet Basket: $910 16 stores were surveyed Nhulunbuy (East Arnhem) Major supermarket Healthy Food Basket: $569 Current Diet Basket: $661 District remote store average Healthy Food Basket: $888 Current Diet Basket: $954 4 stores were surveyed Katherine Major supermarket Healthy Food Basket: $552 Current Diet Basket: $676 District remote store average Healthy Food Basket: $863 Current Diet Basket: $925 17 stores were surveyed Alice Springs Major supermarket Healthy Food Basket: $530 Current Diet Basket: $593 District remote store average Healthy Food Basket: $840 Current Diet Basket: $897 21 stores were surveyed Tennant Creek (Barkly) Not surveyed in 2019 Inquiry into food pricing and food security in remote Indigenous communities Submission 36 - Supplementary Submission NIAA | Food prices and accessibility in remote communities: snapshot July 2020 4 The WA Regional Price Index also shows higher food prices in remote regions compared with Perth Sources: Hugo Centre for Population and Housing (2006); Western Australian Government (2019).\nKimberly 112.1 Pilbara 106.1 Goldfields-Esperance 105.1 Mid West 104.7 Gascoyne 104.9 Wheatbelt 99.5 Perth 100 Peel 101.1 South West 100.6 Great Southern 97.0 In 2019, the Western Australian Government collected the prices of goods and services from 39 regional locations (aggregated to nine regions) to construct the Regional Price Index (RPI). As part of the RPI, a food commodities index was measured. Food prices in Perth were based on the average of eight major supermarkets. The index included dairy, cereals, meat and seafood, fruit and vegetables, drinks, snacks and confectionery, other foods, meals out and takeaway foods.\nSimilar food prices were observed across Perth and the surrounding regions in 2019. In the Great Southern region prices were on average 3 per cent lower. In more remote regions of Western Australia, however, average prices were higher by around: • 5 per cent in the Gascoyne, Mid West and Goldfields-Esperance regions • 6 per cent in the Pilbara • 12 per cent in the Kimberley.\nNon-remote Remote, very restricted accessibility Very Remote, very little accessibility Inquiry into food pricing and food security in remote Indigenous communities Submission 36 - Supplementary Submission NIAA | Food prices and accessibility in remote communities: snapshot July 2020 5 Snapshot of current food prices in remote managed stores Remote, very restricted accessibility Very Remote, very little accessibility For the simple basket of goods, the average price across the 47 participating remote managed store locations was around $100 in May/June 2020. Prices ranged from $85 in remote areas to $135 in very remote areas. Broadly, food prices in community stores appeared to increase as the road distance to reach a community increased (as measure by the ARIA+). However, this was not always the case. For some stores, similar prices were observed across a number of remote locations. The average price across the 47 locations was around 39 per cent higher when compared with major supermarkets in capital cities. When compared to a limited selection of smaller supermarkets in remote town centres with larger populations, average community store prices ranged considerably − from 37 per cent higher in South Australia to 16 per cent lower in Western Australia. This highlights the importance of transport routes and local factors to prices across remote communities.\nThe small number and selection of stores means the reported prices are indicative only. The reported prices may not be representative of food prices across all remote communities.\nSources: Hugo Centre for Population and Housing (2006); Unpublished data obtained by NIAA from managed stores and small remote supermarkets (July 2020). The basket of food items was developed based on the availability of brands and in consultation with members of the NIAA Food Security Working Group. Prices were provided by five managed stores companies and a limited selection of smaller supermarkets in remote town centresa. Prices in major cities were collected via major supermarket websites. Pricing data from the managed stores, smaller supermarkets and major city supermarkets was collected between 20 May and 2 July 2020. To compare prices across locations, prices were adjusted where the weight provided was different from that listed for an item.       "raw_content": "[The verdict](#the-verdict)[What's changed in 2026](#whats-changed-in-2026)[Why a split shop wins](#why-a-split-shop-wins)[Where each store is cheapest](#where-each-store-is-cheapest)[Your store-by-store plan](#your-store-by-store-plan)[What this saves in practice](#what-this-saves-in-practice)[When this does NOT apply](#when-this-does-not-apply)[Frequently asked questions](#frequently-asked-questions)[Key takeaways](#key-takeaways)[Related articles](#related-articles)[Sources](#sources)[Disclaimer](#disclaimer)\n\n[Blog](/blog)\n\n# Woolworths vs Coles vs ALDI vs Costco: Australia 2026 Prices\n\n[![Hejia Zhang](https://cloud.shopback.com/shopback/image/fetch/c_scale,c_auto,q_70,f_webp/https://cloud.shopback.com/image/upload/v1780629399/Blog%20Image/Author%20avatar/sg/jia.png)\n\nHejia Zhang\n\nEditor-in-Chief, ShopBack·](/blog/authors/jia)\n\nWoolworths vs Coles vs ALDI vs Costco grocery prices Australia 2026: a breakdown of where Australians save most on staples, produce and household goods.\n\nFour big names, one weekly shop, and a surprising amount of money riding on how you divide it between them. No single store wins every aisle: ALDI owns staples, Costco owns bulk, and Woolworths and Coles trade blows on brands and specials. Between now and early November 2026, with Halloween on 31 October and the Christmas pantry stock-up starting straight after, the decision each week is which store gets which part of the trolley, not whether to switch stores outright. The cheapest outcome comes from treating each as a specialist. Use ShopBack to compare Woolworths and Coles online before you place a delivery order, then split the rest of the list the way this guide lays out. Here is where each one actually saves you the most.\n\n## The verdict\n\nFor Australian families doing a weekly shop in 2026, the most cost-effective strategy is a split shop: ALDI for staples and pantry items, Woolworths or Coles for branded goods and specials. Families shopping exclusively at Woolworths or Coles typically spend $40 to $70/week more than a comparable ALDI-primary basket. Costco is worth the annual membership for households of 4+ who buy in bulk regularly. This does not apply to single-person households or anyone without ALDI access.\n\n> 💡 [Earn cashback on grocery delivery at ShopBack Australia](https://www.shopback.com.au/)\n\n---\n\n## What's changed in 2026\n\nThe Australian grocery market has moved through a busy 18 months since the ACCC opened its Supermarkets Inquiry in early 2024. Key updates for shoppers as of July 2026:\n\n* **ACCC Supermarkets Inquiry final report** was delivered to the Treasurer on 28 February 2025 and [published 21 March 2025](https://www.accc.gov.au/inquiries-and-consultations/finalised-inquiries-and-monitoring/supermarkets-inquiry-2024-25). The report contained 20 recommendations covering pricing transparency, unit-price display consistency, discount-signage rules, supplier bargaining protections, and clearer specials communication. Government and industry implementation is ongoing through 2026 rather than an overnight change on shelves.\n* **Private-label expansion** at Coles and Woolworths has continued through 2025 and 2026, particularly in chilled and pantry lines where ALDI sets the benchmark. Both major supermarkets now stock deeper private-label ranges (Coles Simply, Woolworths Essentials, Homebrand) that narrow the gap to ALDI on staples by 15 to 30% versus the branded equivalent.\n* **Grocery-price inflation** has cooled from its 2022-to-2023 peak but is still running above the Reserve Bank's target headline CPI band on the food-and-non-alcoholic-beverages line. Households are still paying more for the same basket than in early 2023, and the ACCC's inquiry documented that price rises have not fully reversed as input costs eased.\n* **ALDI Australia store footprint** has continued its measured expansion (still no national online delivery in 2026), and its share of the national grocery market was around 9% per the ACCC final report.\n* **Costco Australia** membership remains $65/year for the Gold Star tier at time of writing; the network of warehouses has continued to expand modestly across the eastern seaboard.\n* **Loyalty programs** (Everyday Rewards, flybuys) continue to return roughly 0.5 to 1% of spend in redemption value; the mechanics are unchanged in 2026.\n\nThe practical takeaway for 2026: the ranking of who is cheapest has not shifted, but the tools to prove it (unit pricing, discount claims, specials clarity) are becoming more consistent as the ACCC recommendations flow through.\n\n> Save on grocery delivery through ShopBack: [Woolworths](https://www.shopback.com.au/woolworths) · [Coles](https://www.shopback.com.au/coles) · [Amazon Australia](https://www.shopback.com.au/amazon-australia) · [iHerb](https://www.shopback.com.au/iherb)\n\n---\n\n## Why a split shop wins\n\nThe **Supermarket Split Strategy** treats each store as a specialist rather than a one-stop shop. ALDI prices are structurally lower because it carries ~1,800 SKUs (vs Woolworths' 30,000+) and sources most of its range under private label. Woolworths and Coles compete on promotions, loyalty points, and specials, which can make specific branded items cheaper on any given week.\n\nWoolworths vs Coles is essentially a price tie, their pricing algorithms track each other closely. The [ACCC's 2025 Supermarkets Inquiry](https://www.accc.gov.au/media-release/accc-recommends-supermarket-reforms-to-provide-better-outcomes-for-consumers-and-suppliers) reached the same conclusion structurally, finding that Coles and Woolworths (together about two-thirds of national grocery sales) have limited incentive to compete vigorously with each other on price. The decision between them is better made on location, delivery service, and loyalty program preference.\n\n> Compare cashback on the majors: [Woolworths](https://www.shopback.com.au/woolworths) · [Coles](https://www.shopback.com.au/coles) · [Amazon Australia](https://www.shopback.com.au/amazon-australia) · [iHerb](https://www.shopback.com.au/iherb)\n\n---\n\n## Where each store is cheapest\n\n| Category | Cheapest Option | Typical Saving vs Woolworths/Coles |\n| --- | --- | --- |\n| Dry pasta, rice, canned goods | ALDI | 25 to 40% |\n| Bread and bakery | ALDI | 20 to 35% |\n| Dairy (milk, butter, cheese) | ALDI or Costco | 15 to 30% |\n| Fresh produce | ALDI or Woolworths specials | 10 to 20% |\n| Branded cereals and snacks | Coles/Woolworths on special | Variable |\n| Cleaning products (bulk) | Costco | 30 to 50% vs unit price |\n| Meat (bulk packs) | Costco | 20 to 35% |\n| Organic / specialty items | Woolworths or Coles | ALDI doesn't stock most |\n\nThe numbers show that the 20 to 30% ALDI advantage on staples translates to roughly $40 to $70/week for a family of four, more than enough to justify an extra stop.\n\n> Save on household basics: [Big W](https://www.shopback.com.au/big-w) · [Target](https://www.shopback.com.au/target-australia) · [Amazon Australia](https://www.shopback.com.au/amazon-australia) · [iHerb](https://www.shopback.com.au/iherb)\n\n---\n\n## Your store-by-store plan\n\n**Rule:** Use ALDI for weekly pantry staples and basic fresh produce. Use Woolworths or Coles for branded items and whatever's on special that week. Consider Costco monthly if you have a household of 4+ and adequate storage.\n\n| Household Type | Best Strategy | Est. Annual Saving vs Coles/Woolworths-only |\n| --- | --- | --- |\n| Family of 4, metro with ALDI | ALDI-primary + Coles/Woolworths specials | $2,000 to $3,500 |\n| Family of 4, Costco access | ALDI + Costco monthly | $2,500 to $4,000 |\n| Couple, $150/week shop | ALDI-primary | $800 to $1,500 |\n| Single person, $80/week | Either, proximity wins | $300 to $600 |\n| Regional with no ALDI | Coles/Woolworths + weekly specials | Limited switching benefit |\n\n---\n\n## What this saves in practice\n\n**For Woolworths and Coles online grocery orders, going through ShopBack before you pay is the step that earns Cashback on the order.**\n\nIn practice, this means: a family of four currently spending $280/week at Woolworths exclusively can realistically reduce that to $200 to $220 by shifting 60% to ALDI and buying Coles/Woolworths specials for the rest. That's a meaningful annual saving from a two-stop shop adding 15 to 20 minutes per week.\n\nA typical trade-off: ALDI 1L full-cream milk at ~$1.79 vs branded milk at $2.60 to $3.20. For a family going through 6 to 8 litres/week, that difference adds up to hundreds of dollars annually on milk alone.\n\n---\n\n## When this does NOT apply\n\n* **No ALDI within reasonable distance:** The split-shop saving disappears if the detour costs time or fuel equivalent to the price difference.\n* **Single-person households on small budgets:** The absolute dollar saving from a split shop is $10 to $20/week, may not justify two stops.\n* **Specialty dietary requirements:** ALDI's limited range often doesn't cover gluten-free, vegan specialty, or specific health food categories.\n* **Online-only shoppers:** ALDI doesn't offer home delivery; the split strategy requires at least one in-store visit.\n* **Costco memberships for small households:** A couple buying standard quantities may not consume bulk purchases before expiry.\n\n> Compare cashback on grocery delivery: [Woolworths](https://www.shopback.com.au/woolworths) · [Coles](https://www.shopback.com.au/coles) · [Amazon Australia](https://www.shopback.com.au/amazon-australia) · [Big W](https://www.shopback.com.au/big-w)\n\n---\n\n## Frequently asked questions\n\nIs ALDI cheaper than Coles and Woolworths for a full weekly shop?\n\nYes, ALDI is typically 20 to 30% cheaper than Coles or Woolworths on comparable staples. However, ALDI's limited range means most households use it alongside another supermarket.\n\nIs Costco worth it for Australian families?\n\nFor households of 4 or more who buy in bulk regularly, the annual membership typically pays for itself within a few visits. Smaller households may not use bulk quantities before expiry.\n\nIs there a meaningful price difference between Woolworths and Coles?\n\nGenerally no, on an equivalent basket, Woolworths and Coles are typically within 2 to 4% of each other. Choose based on location, delivery preference, and loyalty program.\n\nDoes Woolworths or Coles have a better loyalty program?\n\nBoth Everyday Rewards and Flybuys return roughly 0.5 to 1% in points value. The better program is whichever one you'll actually redeem, unclaimed points return nothing.\n\nIs ALDI produce as good quality as Coles and Woolworths?\n\nALDI produce quality is generally comparable for common vegetables and fruit, though the range is more limited.\n\nCan you do a full weekly shop at ALDI in Australia?\n\nNot easily, ALDI covers staples well but lacks most branded goods and specialty items. Most households use it alongside another supermarket.\n\nDoes ALDI offer home delivery in Australia?\n\nNo, ALDI does not offer home delivery in Australia. For grocery delivery, Woolworths and Coles are the main options.\n\nHow much is a Costco membership in Australia?\n\nCostco membership is currently $65 per year for a standard (Gold Star) membership, subject to change. Check [Costco Australia's website](https://www.costco.com.au/membership) for the current fee.\n\nWhat did the ACCC Supermarkets Inquiry find, and what's changed for Australian shoppers in 2026?\n\nThe ACCC delivered its [final Supermarkets Inquiry (2024-25) report](https://www.accc.gov.au/inquiries-and-consultations/finalised-inquiries-and-monitoring/supermarkets-inquiry-2024-25) to the Treasurer on 28 February 2025, published 21 March 2025. The final report confirmed the market is highly concentrated (Woolworths ~38%, Coles ~29%, ALDI ~9%, other independents ~24% combined) and that Coles and Woolworths have limited incentive to compete vigorously with each other on price. Twenty recommendations spanned pricing transparency, supplier bargaining relationships, and consumer clarity around specials and unit pricing. Implementation is ongoing through 2026; the shopping impact for households is incremental rather than immediate.\n\nAre private-label ranges expanding in Coles and Woolworths in 2026?\n\nYes. Both Coles (Coles Own Brand, Coles Finest, Coles Simply) and Woolworths (Woolworths Essentials, Homebrand, Macro, Woolworths Gold) have continued expanding private-label depth through 2025 and 2026, particularly in fresh, chilled, and pantry categories where ALDI historically sets the private-label benchmark. Private-label substitution at Coles or Woolworths typically saves 15 to 30% on those items versus the branded equivalent, closing but not eliminating the gap to ALDI on staples.\n\nIs Costco worth joining in 2026 given ALDI is nearby?\n\nCostco and ALDI solve different problems. ALDI wins on weekly staple pricing and requires no membership. Costco wins on bulk unit pricing across household, cleaning, non-perishable pantry, and dairy for families of 4 or more with storage space. If you already have an ALDI within 15 minutes, Costco adds value only if you consume enough bulk quantities in a month to clear the $65 annual membership plus the drive time.\n\nHow can I earn cashback on grocery delivery through ShopBack?\n\nActivate ShopBack, then click through to [Woolworths](https://www.shopback.com.au/woolworths) or [Coles](https://www.shopback.com.au/coles) and complete the delivery order in one session.
